Multiagent Systems.summary: Assigning routine tasks to cheaper large language model (LLM) providers can reduce generation cost, but switching providers may require processing accumulated context again. Keeping dependent tasks with the same provider can instead reuse eligible context. Graph-based workflows therefore couple routing decisions across tasks. Independent providers may also privately know their real-time unit costs and strategically misreport them. We formulate this routing problem as a single-parameter procurement auction and propose STAR (Strategy-proof Topology-aware Agent Routing), which minimizes virtual-cost-weighted graph workloads. Its allocation rule and payments, computed by integrating workload over possible cost reports, make truthful reporting utility-maximizing regardless of other providers' reports and cover each truthful provider's execution cost. With independent cost distributions and non-decreasing virtual costs, STAR additionally minimizes the user's expected total payment to providers. Controlled synthetic experiments separate the execution-cost benefit of topology awareness from the payment benefit of virtual-cost optimization: the former grows with fan-out and transferred payload, while the latter increases gradually along the tested prior-shape heterogeneity path. A paired sensitivity study quantifies how payment savings vary with prior misspecification while strategy-proofness is preserved.

Multiagent Systems.title: LLM-as-an-Investigator: Evidence-First Agentic Reasoning for Robust Interactive Problem Diagnosis
Multiagent Systems.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are used for technical troubleshooting, where problem descriptions are often incomplete and multiple causes can explain the same symptoms. Effective diagnosis requires acquiring discriminative evidence and selecting the explanation best supported by it. Yet reasoning or interaction alone may not prevent premature commitment to an incorrect hypothesis. We introduce LLM-as-an-Investigator, an evidence-first methodology for interactive problem diagnosis that reduces premature commitment while distinguishing competing causes. We implement it through the Solution Investigator Agent (SIA), which orchestrates three complementary reasoning behaviours through a shared investigation state: a Diagnostic Reasoner that conducts and reassesses the diagnostic interview, a Hypothesis Investigator that maintains and updates competing hypotheses, and a Counterfactual Investigator that challenges current explanations and guides discriminative follow-up questions. Final selection uses cited dialogue evidence and a separate verification step, while explicit hypothesis and evidence records make the diagnosis traceable and preserve unresolved alternatives. We construct a structured corpus from 303 technical forum threads across mechanical, electrical, and hydraulic domains. A source-grounded pipeline separates the initial problem, pre-solution clarifications, and reported outcome, while a user simulator answers diagnostic questions without access to the reference solution. We compare SIA with direct, reasoning-based, interactive, and search-based baselines, including adaptations of ReAct and Tree of Thoughts. Evaluation distinguishes final diagnostic quality from hypothesis coverage and oracle potential, while ablations and paired stress tests assess component contributions and robustness to plausible but misleading user hypotheses.

Multiagent Systems.title: Narrowing the Collaboration Gap, Probably
Multiagent Systems.summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as teams of agents that hold different private information about a shared task. How should such agents concisely communicate in a way that promotes aggregation of decision-relevant information? Communicating only proposed actions can discard decision-relevant uncertainty: two agents may prefer the same action for different reasons. We study an alternative interface in which agents communicate calibrated beliefs over actions. We first analyze a simple synthetic setting that captures the structure of multi-round reasoning under partial information. In this setting, we show theoretically and empirically that communicating unbiased probabilities can be strictly more powerful than communicating actions. We then test the same principle in a collaborative maze-solving task with trained transformers and pretrained LLM agents. Our results demonstrate that probability communication outperforms action communication when the exchanged predictions preserve calibrated uncertainty. When communicated probabilities are biased, we show that the benefits of probability communication can disappear. We give a post-hoc conversational calibration intervention that consistently improves decision-making by correcting these biases both in a toy transformer setting and when pretrained LLMs use the corrections in context. These results suggest that probabilistic communication is useful for multi-agent collaboration not merely because it transmits more information, but because calibrated uncertainty gives other agents a reliable object to update on.

Multiagent Systems.title: Kalman-Bucy Filtering with Randomized Sensing: Fundamental Limits and Sensor Network Design for Field Estimation
Multiagent Systems.summary: Stability analysis of the Kalman filter under randomly lost measurements has been widely studied. We revisit this problem in a general continuous-time framework, where both the measurement matrix and noise covariance evolve as random processes, capturing variability in sensing locations. Within this setting, we derive a closed-form upper bound on the expected estimation covariance for continuous-time Kalman filtering. We then apply this framework to spatiotemporal field estimation, where the field is modeled as a Gaussian process observed by randomly located, noisy sensors. Using clarity, introduced in our earlier work as a rescaled form of the differential entropy of a random variable, we establish a lower bound on the expected spatially averaged clarity and show that its steady-state value converges to a grid-independent limit as the grid is refined. This result exposes fundamental performance limits through a composite sensing parameter that jointly captures the effects of the number of sensors, noise level, and measurement frequency. Simulations show close agreement between the continuous-time analytical solution and the discrete-time covariance, with the agreement improving as the sampling interval decreases. The analytical solution also avoids the recursive computations required in the discrete-time formulation. Most importantly, the derived limits provide principled and efficient guidelines for sensor network design prior to deployment.

Multiagent Systems.title: CLASHarness: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Conflict in Computer Use via a Controllable and Verifiable Generation Pipeline
Multiagent Systems.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems to automate complex computer-use workflows, yet existing benchmarks mostly assume consistent, cooperative environments. In contrast, real-world collaboration rarely runs on consistent information: peer or sub-agents frequently report outdated states, issue contradictory instructions, or compete over shared permissions and files, forcing agents to check others' outputs and verify ground truth in the environment. Evaluating such conflict resolution remains challenging: manual authoring cannot scale across complex systems, while unconstrained LLM generation produces narrative drift, answer leakage, and unsatisfiable rubrics. We introduce CLASHarness (Conflict-Loaded Agent Scenario Harness), a controllable framework for generating verifiable multi-agent conflicts in computer use, with a benchmark of 600 multi-round tasks. By combining hierarchical scenario planning with an eight-step verified micro-pipeline, CLASHarness pre-commits decisive visual facts before rendering and compiles hybrid code and semantic graders directly from executed reference trajectories, guaranteeing every task is solvable by construction. Evaluating 15 frontier models on CLASHarness reveals three core bottlenecks. First, when sub-agent outputs conflict with the environment, weaker models blindly follow misleading information, whereas stronger models inspect visual evidence to verify ground truth. Second, resolving conflicts is much harder than finding them: while agents can spot inconsistencies, actively fixing system state drops task success significantly. Third, coordination protocols remain a universal bottleneck: even frontier models fail over 58% of closing actions, often forgetting to release shared locks or hand off tasks. CLASHarness provides a scalable, verifiable foundation for building reliable multi-agent systems.

Multiagent Systems.title: Fake Plastic Voters: When Political Parties Can Use AI-Simulated Focus Groups
Multiagent Systems.summary: Political parties strive to understand their electorates, and focus groups are a vital tool in these efforts. AI-enhanced simulation technologies (AESTs) enable synthetic focus groups in a fraction of the time (and cost), raising the question of when and how such simulated evidence can be used in campaign research. This paper develops a decision matrix to help party strategists match research needs to appropriate simulation technologies and to identify when to escalate to hybrid or fully human focus groups. The matrix combines three dimensions: strategic purpose, deployment risk, and empirical grounding of the simulation tool. Strategic purpose is the decisive dimension, as it determines what kind of evidence the focus group is meant to produce: observing how political meanings and identities emerge through interaction (Mode 1) or testing and refining campaign messages (Mode 2). The matrix shows that, given documented failure modes such as sycophancy, persona drift, and the suppression of minority viewpoints, AESTs cannot replace human interaction in Mode 1 at any risk level. Within Mode 2, suitability depends instead on deployment risk and on the empirical grounding. Yet even here, we caution that routine reliance on AESTs may erode the qualitative craft on which sound judgment depends.

Multiagent Systems.title: Smart Alone, Blind Together: Why Accuracy Fails to CertifyTheory of Mind in Multi-Agent Teams
Multiagent Systems.summary: Coordinators that act on what they infer about teammates are usually certified by the accuracy of those inferences. We argue that accuracy is the wrong certificate, for two reasons. First, the accuracy needed to act depends on what a wrong action costs, so the bar belongs to the deployment, not the module. Second, a module's errors are rarely independent, and dependence has a sign: positively associated errors help where their damage overlaps and hurt where it compounds, so an accuracy threshold fails in a predictable direction, and once wrong beliefs interact and can do harm, no rule based on accuracy is right for every module. We test these predictions in task assignment, Level-Based Foraging and Hanabi, with injected errors, trained and Bayesian modules and five language models, and in human judgments. Accuracy fails in both directions, approving harmful language-model deployments in Hanabi, where shared errors compound, and rejecting beneficial ones in task assignment, where costly errors are rare. In our tasks it also buys far less redundancy than independence predicts: from GPT-5.4-mini to Claude Opus 5.5, error on teammates the models have evidence about falls from 32% to 11%, but the chance that all three observers misread one falls only from 16% to 9% (independence: 3.4% to 0.15%). We propose certifying the deployment, with a Blind-Spot Gate that prices error costs, pairwise interactions and measured dependence without deploying the module. On held-out data from the cells it was developed on, it makes no significant false approval in 20 splits (accuracy: 3.2 per split), and in preregistered tests on modules it was not developed on, it recovers what accuracy rejects (seven classifiers: regret 0.004 against 0.479) and catches what accuracy approves (a Bayesian module: significant false approvals in 17 of 20 splits for accuracy, 1 for the gate).

Multiagent Systems.title: How Far Are We From True Auto-Research?
Multiagent Systems.summary: Recent auto-research systems can produce complete papers, but feasibility is not the same as quality, and the field still lacks a systematic study of how good agent-generated papers actually are. We introduce ResearchArena, a minimal scaffold that lets off-the-shelf agents (Claude Code using Opus 4.6, Codex using GPT-5.4, and Kimi Code using K2.5) carry out the full research loop themselves (ideation, experimentation, paper writing, self-refinement) under only lightweight guidance. Across 13 computer science seeds and 3 trials per agent-domain pair, ResearchArena yields 117 agent-generated papers, each evaluated under three complementary lenses: a manuscript-only reviewer (SAR), an artifact-aware peer review (PR) in which agents inspect the workspace alongside the manuscript, and an human conducted meta-review. Under SAR alone the picture is optimistic: Claude Code obtains the highest score, outperforms Analemma's FARS, and matches the weighted-average human ICLR 2025 submission, suggesting that minimally scaffolded agents can produce papers that look competitive on manuscript-only review. Manual inspection, however, reveals this picture is overstated: SAR scores are poorly aligned with its actual acceptance decisions and reward plausible framing without verifying experimental substance. Under artifact-aware PR scores drop sharply, and manual auditing identifies experimental rigor as the major bottleneck, decomposing into three failure modes (fabricated results, underpowered experiments, and plan/execution mismatch) that are highly agent-dependent: Codex 5%/8% paper-vs-artifact mismatch / fabricated references versus Kimi Code 77%/72%, a $\sim$15$\times$ spread that tracks distinct research personas the agents develop. None of the 117 agent-generated papers reaches the acceptance bar of a top-tier venue. This suggests that we are still gapped from the true auto-research.

Multiagent Systems.title: Prompt Stability Matters: Evaluating and Optimizing Auto-Generated Prompt in General-Purpose Systems
Multiagent Systems.summary: Automatic prompt generation plays a crucial role in enabling general-purpose multi-agent systems to perform diverse tasks autonomously. Existing methods typically evaluate prompts based on their immediate task performance, overlooking the intrinsic qualities that determine their reliability. This outcome-centric view not only limits interpretability but also fails to account for the inherent stochasticity of large language models (LLMs). In this work, we bring attention to prompt stability-the consistency of model responses across repeated executions-as a key factor for building robust and effective prompt generation systems. To quantify this, we propose semantic stability as a criterion for assessing the response consistency of prompts. Based on the proposed metric, we developed the first stability-aware general-purpose prompt generation system that leverages stability feedback to iteratively enhance both prompt quality and system-level performance. Furthermore, we establish a logical chain between prompt stability and task success by analyzing the structural dependencies within our system, proving stability as a necessary condition for effective system-level execution. Empirical results across general and domain-specific tasks demonstrate that our stability-aware framework improves both accuracy and output consistency. By shifting the focus from one-off results to persistent reliability, our work offers a new perspective on prompt design and contributes practical tools for building more trustworthy general-purpose systems. The UI and source code for our system are publicly available at: https://xucheng63.github.io/MyDataPilot/.

Multiagent Systems.title: CyberArena: Benchmarking AI Agents in Live Symmetric Attack-and-Defense Combat
Multiagent Systems.summary: AI agents are demonstrating increasingly strong offensive and defensive cybersecurity capabilities in the real world. Current benchmarks mostly evaluate agents in isolation against static targets. Real cyber operations, however, are dynamic and coupled: security postures constantly change as attackers and defenders adapt to each other in real time. Static benchmarks quickly saturate and miss an agent's ability to attack and defend simultaneously under live pressure. To address this gap, we present CyberArena, a dynamic, symmetric adversarial benchmark built around multi-round attack-and-defense combat. In isolated sandboxes, two agents compete under identical rules, acting concurrently as both attackers and defenders over continuously changing services. This converts static targets into evolving, semi-open challenges, directly testing an agent's speed and precision in discovering, exploiting, and patching vulnerabilities. To sustain the benchmark's longevity, an automated agentic pipeline continuously generates, reviews, and validates new environments. Furthermore, because pairwise contests are notoriously hard to quantify, we introduce a dynamical model that maps match dynamics into unified, multidimensional scores across offensive, defensive, and domain-specific capabilities. Evaluating 12 frontier LLM agents across 40 challenges in 466 matches, CyberArena separates model capabilities where single-agent baselines hit a ceiling. The trajectories read like a fight rather than an exam: defenders patch one hole and miss the next and certify repairs on stale evidence, while capable agents think a move ahead, planting backdoors for later rounds and, in one case, writing their own packet sniffer to watch the opponent. Beyond a benchmark, CyberArena serves as an adaptable, scalable experimental platform for future research on cybersecurity agents.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Optimizing Team Behavior via Extremum-seeking Control in Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents must learn to coordinate their actions to achieve shared objectives. A key indicator of effective coordination is behavioral diversity, i.e., the agents' potential to enact distinct yet complementary control policies given the same set of observations. Although behavioral diversity can enable role specialization and richer joint behaviors, its appropriate level is highly context- and task-dependent and often costly to tune. We propose Adaptive Diversity Control (ADiCo), a two-timescale framework that adapts behavioral diversity online during training. On a fast timescale, Diversity Control (DiCo) regulates system diversity toward a target value. On a slower timescale, an Extremum Seeking Controller (ESC) adjusts this target using only mean episodic returns, without requiring an explicit model or analytical gradient of the diversity-performance landscape. We evaluate ADiCo on six configurations across two cooperative MARL tasks, where it maintains task-appropriate diversity levels: low diversity when homogeneous policies are beneficial and higher diversity when heterogeneous policies are required. Through this adaptation, ADiCo matches or exceeds the mean performance of DiCo (best grid-searched diversity target) and Unconstrained DiCo (diversity allowed to emerge without target regulation). These results demonstrate that incorporating classical feedback control into MARL training enables effective coordination by providing a systematic alternative to task-specific manual selection of the diversity target.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: Accepted for publication at the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC 2026), Hawaii, USA

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Compositional Sensitivity Analysis for Multiobjective System Co-Design
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Sensitivity analysis of coupled systems typically propagates derivatives of single-valued maps, whereas multiobjective optimization generally treats sensitivity at the system level rather than through interconnected subsystems. We develop a mathematical framework for compositional sensitivity analysis in multiobjective system design, building on monotone co-design. Subsystems are represented as design problems (DPs), interconnected through series, parallel, union, intersection, and feedback composition. We introduce tangential DPs (TDPs) to describe first-order variations around an operating point, show that they preserve the structure of DPs, and characterize their queries through graphical derivatives. To account for multiple internal realizations of a system-level operating point, tangential co-design problems compose families of local TDPs by taking a union over these realizations while retaining the original interconnection structure. We show that these compositions yield families of TDPs and establish conditions under which sensitivity analysis commutes with individual composition operations. Beyond infinitesimal sensitivity, we show that bounded tangential models of convex DPs provide tighter outer approximations of feasible finite changes, which can be propagated through co-design problems without union compositions. We conclude with several convex and nonconvex numerical examples that showcase the framework's accuracy and computational benefits.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: MagCeptor: Encoding Broadcast-Addressable Logic into Magnetic Receptors
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Selectively operating multiple components while simplifying actuation and control hardware is a common challenge in multifunctional mechanical and fluidic systems. Here, we introduce MagCeptor, an addressable magnetic-cluster architecture in which a shared external field conveys commands and supplies actuation energy. Fixed stators establish local magnetic-field gradients, while field-induced mover reorientation modulates the resulting forces to select guide-constrained mechanical outputs. Field-dependent position-orientation energy profiles explain target actuation, non-target retention and passive reset after field removal. The evaluated configuration achieves a maximum normalized force output of 385 mN/mm3. By coupling finite, addressable strokes to mechanical transmissions, accumulators and locks, we demonstrate coordinated rotation and multistep manipulation with retained task states. Hierarchical node-and-channel addressing further enables selective model-fluid release from distributed receivers in ex vivo tissue. These results establish a receiver-side architecture that combines shared magnetic inputs with task-specific mechanisms to organize mechanical work, retain operation states and access spatially distributed functions.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Dynamic Attack Surfaces: A Queue of Branching Processes
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Modern attack surfaces are inherently dynamic. Vulnerabilities emerge over time and they remain exposed to exploit until defenders discover and patch them. Artificial intelligence (AI) amplifies these dynamics by accelerating both offensive and defensive processes, making modern cybersecurity increasingly a competition among interacting time scales and resources. We capture this competition using a queue of branching processes that couples vulnerability discovery and resource-constrained patching with the evolving attacker population targeting each vulnerability. Our primary risk metric is the cumulative number of exploits a vulnerability experiences before it is patched. We derive the expected cumulative number of exploits under birth-death-immigration (BDI) and rise-decay (RD) models of attacker activity. Under a BDI model of attacker activity, we identify a phase transition: the expected cumulative number of exploits is finite only when attacker growth remains below both the vulnerability discovery rate and the effective patching rate. Across both attacker models, increasing the exploit rate does not necessarily increase the expected number of exploits because faster attacker departure can sufficiently limit the active attacker population. Finally, we show that equal proportional AI amplification of offensive and defensive capabilities need not preserve security: accelerating both sides can shift the defensive bottleneck and move the system into an unbounded-risk regime.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Rethinking electrified transportation: The case for dynamic wireless charging
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Long-term infrastructure investment often requires choosing between an established technology and a capital-intensive alternative that gains value as demand matures. For electric vehicle (EV) charging, this trade-off is between incumbent stationary charging technology and emerging dynamic wireless charging (DWC). DWC could fundamentally alter transportation electrification by enabling high-throughput charging in motion and reducing reliance on large onboard batteries; however, its high upfront cost makes the timing and location of deployment critical. Overcommitting to stationary charging stations (SCS) risks technological lock-in and forgoing the benefits of DWC, whereas premature DWC deployment can strand capital in underutilized corridors. Through a joint investment assessment framework coupling DWC, SCS, and supporting grid infrastructure across nearly 49,000 miles of the US Interstate freight network, we find that higher utilization and longer project lifetimes rapidly shift investment toward DWC, whose share rises sharply from 48% at a project lifetime of 30 years to 100% at 32 years. Contiguous DWC segments can share grid connections, enabling them to provide over six times the rated charging capacity of SCS while requiring 46% less investment in new distribution-grid infrastructure. We also find that a combined DWC and SCS portfolio reaches a maximum lifetime value of USD 60 billion, 63% above the case with only SCS. We further identify specific traffic demand, construction, and grid access conditions that shape where each technology becomes advantageous, yielding actionable thresholds for SCS and DWC deployment that directly inform long-term EV charging infrastructure investment and policy.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: High-Order Matrix Control Barrier Functions: Well-Posedness and Feasibility via Matrix Relative Degree
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide an effective framework for enforcing safety in dynamical systems with scalar constraints. However, many safety constraints are more naturally expressed as matrix-valued conditions, such as positive definiteness or eigenvalue bounds - scalar formulations introduce potential nonsmoothness that complicates analysis. Matrix control barrier functions (MCBFs) address this limitation by directly enforcing matrix-valued safety constraints. Yet for constraints where the control input does not appear in the first derivative, high-order formulations are required. While such extensions are well understood in the scalar case, they remain largely unexplored in the matrix case. This paper develops high-order matrix control barrier functions (HOMCBFs) and establishes conditions ensuring well-posedness and feasibility of the associated constraints, enabling enforcement of matrix-valued safety constraints for systems with high-order dynamics. We further show that, using an optimal-decay HOMCBF formulation, forward invariance can be ensured while requiring control only over the minimum eigenspace. The framework is demonstrated on a double-integrator localization problem by enforcing positive definiteness of the information matrix.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Model-Based Online Decision Making via Generative Trajectory Planning
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Online decision-making faces a tension between efficient inference and long-horizon reasoning. Value-based methods rely on short-horizon bootstrapping that limits the propagation of long-term information, while trajectory optimization methods plan explicitly but must solve a high-dimensional optimization problem at every decision step. We propose Generative Trajectory Planning (GTP), a model-based framework that addresses this tension by learning a generative model as a proposal distribution over action sequences. Instead of optimizing sequences from scratch, GTP samples candidate sequences from a diffusion prior and refines them using learned dynamics, reward, and value models, enabling efficient trajectory-level reasoning. Across continuous control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, GTP matches or exceeds state-of-the-art model-free, diffusion-policy, and model-based baselines, and remains stable in regimes where strong baselines degrade. Our results suggest that generative models are best understood not as policies, but as structured proposal distributions for planning, offering a new perspective on how to integrate generative modeling with model-based decision-making.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Time-Invariant Linear Quadratic Regulators: A New Look
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper demonstrates that linear ordinary differential equations with constant coefficients serve as the main building block for time-invariant linear quadratic regulators (LQRs). By applying the Euler-Lagrange equations to a flat output, i.e., to a basis of the free finitely-generated module over the commutative principal ideal ring of time-invariant linear differential operators with respect to the time derivation, this result emerges directly. In module-theoretic terms. The freeness of this structure corresponds to the classical Kalman controllability condition (M. Fliess, Some basic structural properties of generalized linear systems, Syst. Contr. Lett., 15 (1990) 391-396). Within this framework, the two-point boundary value problem, including the control variables, becomes analytically tractable, enabling the derivation of optimal time horizons, optimal parameter design, and rest-to-rest trajectories. Furthermore, a novel turnpike-like phenomenon is established via nonstandard analysis. The feedback loop is closed thanks to the HEOL approach (C. Join, E. Delaleau, M. Fliess, Flatness-based control revisited: The HEOL setting, C.R. Math., 362 (2024) 1693-1706), an extension of model-free control (MFC) that leverages intelligent controllers. Our viewpoint, which significantly simplifies the presentation by avoiding the conventional Kalman state-space representation, relies on foundational algebraic concepts that, while elementary, are rarely used in today's control theory. To aid intuition, some rudimentary examples are presented, most of which include computer simulations.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Optimal Decay Matrix Control Barrier Functions: Soundness and Completeness for Matrix Safety Constraints
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Many safety requirements, such as keeping a manipulator away from kinematic singularities, a network connected, or a system observable, amount to keeping a state-dependent matrix positive definite. Matrix control barrier functions (MCBFs) enforce such requirements with a semidefinite program that minimally modifies a nominal control input. The MCBF constraint bounds how fast the safety margin, the smallest eigenvalue of the matrix, may decay. Yet a fixed decay rule is conservative, rejecting safe controls that drive the state quickly toward, but never across, the boundary of the safe set. Scalar optimal decay (SOD) addresses this issue by scaling the decay term by a scalar weight that is optimized together with the control. For scalar barrier functions, SOD then rejects a control at the boundary only if the control would decrease the margin. For MCBFs, however, SOD can reject controls that leave the margin unchanged, and near the safety boundary SOD accepts such controls only at a high cost. We introduce matrix optimal decay (MOD), which replaces the scalar weight with a matrix multiplier while keeping the semidefinite program convex. MOD is provably sound and complete, certifying at the boundary exactly the controls that do not decrease the margin. If some control can strictly increase the margin at every boundary point, the MOD-MCBF filtered controller is continuous and renders the safe set forward invariant. We also add an optional recovery condition that drives the system toward the safe set after a violation without affecting soundness or completeness. On a planar two-link arm avoiding singularities, MOD-MCBF certifies safe motions that both a fixed decay rule and SOD reject, and tracks an end-effector target more closely than SOD.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Instantaneous Frequency in Power Systems using the Teager-Kaiser Energy Operator
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This letter develops an instantaneous-frequency (IF) local estimator calculated with the complex Teager--Kaiser energy operator (CTKEO) and the dynamic-signal identity. The contribution is a novel CTKEO-based IF expression that makes the envelope-curvature terms explicit, thus correcting the bias that affects conventional estimators used in power systems. The estimator aligns with complex-frequency (CF) kinematics and admits a geometric interpretation (curvature) without phase unwrapping. This yields an accurate local frequency estimate in operating conditions where magnitude variations contribute non-negligibly to the signal dynamics. Tests on field measurements illustrate the practical behavior of the proposed approach and its consistency with a geometric-frequency benchmark.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Dynamic Programming for A Linear-Gaussian Dual Control Problem
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We consider an infinite-horizon discounted dynamic programming (DP) problem for a countable-innovation belief-state model. The model is a surrogate for a linear-Gaussian dual control problem involving an unknown parameter vector and Gaussian observation noise. The surrogate preserves the first two moments of the Gaussian innovation and the resulting posterior second-moment structure. We allow unbounded belief and control spaces and nonnegative stage costs with quadratic growth in the posterior mean and covariance. Using a posterior-moment weight, we show that the Bellman operator is a contraction in a weighted sup-norm space. We characterize the optimal cost as the unique solution of the Bellman equation in this space, establish the existence of optimal stationary policies. We further prove weighted sup-norm convergence of value iteration, policy iteration, and optimistic policy iteration under vanishing approximation errors. The convergence results under vanishing approximation errors rely on general weighted sup-norm contraction properties and are applicable beyond the particular dual control problem considered here.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: AgentStripes: An Evidence-Graded Maturity Model for AI Agents
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Benchmarks report what an Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent can do on a task suite, but not whether one released version has been engineered with the controls that make it reliable, safe and observable, or how strongly that is shown. This paper proposes AgentStripes, an evidence-graded maturity model for AI agents. It defines levels (0 to 7 stripes), process areas (12 areas holding 40 capabilities), three gates (basic, safety, proof) that hold an agent at a level however high its score, and evidence grades E0 to E5. Each applicable capability receives a rating from 0 to 3 and a separate evidence level; these are combined into a credit, aggregated into a severity-weighted score and converted into stripes that the gates limit. Instruments gather evidence, language-model judges interpret it under explicit criteria, and the arithmetic is deterministic. The model is compared with standards at topic level without a claim of conformance, and an unexecuted validation protocol is specified. An empirical evaluation (exploratory, non-confirmatory) of 30 public Python agent repositories, with static evidence only, is a demonstration and not a validation: static evidence caps every final stripe at 2, 26 repositories end at one stripe and 4 at two, and this distinction is unreliable, since re-judging changed the final stripe of 4 of 22 repositories (engine, dossier and panel changed), whereas none of 8 panel-only repeats, all at stripe 1, changed. The parameters are expert conventions without outcome based calibration, and the stripes have not been shown to predict reliability or safety.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 32 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables, 116 references; supplementary information (15 pages, 8 figures, 21 tables) included in the same PDF. Code and data available on request

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Shadow Pricing in Transient Stability-Constrained Optimal Power Flow
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Transient stability constraints alter the economic dispatch of power systems, while the resulting price signals and their implications for market settlement remain insufficiently characterized. Existing approaches identify stability-related components in locational marginal prices, without deriving shadow prices for individual assets, such as generators and loads, or analyzing the resulting settlement. To address this gap, this paper derives shadow prices from a transient stability-constrained optimal power flow in which the differential-algebraic equations governing the system dynamics are embedded through direct discretization. Each shadow price decomposes into a nodal energy component and a stability component, the latter formed by the dual variables of the dynamic equations in which the power of the asset appears. Shadow prices are therefore asset-specific: co-located generators and loads are assigned the same nodal energy component, but can be subject to different stability components when their transient behaviors differ. Case studies on the WECC 9-bus system and a modified IEEE 39-bus system show that settlement at the proposed shadow prices allocates the cost of the stability constraints among the assets without any side payment. An asset that reduces the stability margin is charged its stability component, whereas an asset that improves it is paid, and no generator is dispatched at a loss.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Online learning of neural state-space models
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Recent advances in deep-learning-based nonlinear system identification have led to encoder-based estimation of neural state-space (ANN-SS) models that achieve state-of-the-art performance in offline settings by estimating initial model states from past input-output data. These methods are typically used in multiple-shooting-based offline identification, and online learning of these models remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a batch-wise learning pipeline and a direct recursive identification algorithm for subspace encoder-based ANN-SS models. We provide convergence analysis of the recursive formulation and validate its performance through extensive simulation studies. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach enables computationally efficient online adaptation with high model accuracy.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: Accepted to IEEE L-CSS. Extended version (original paper does not contain Fig. 1, Eq. (16), (17) and related discussions)

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Ensemble-MIX: Enhancing Sample-Efficiency in Multi-Agent RL via Selective Ensemble-Based Exploration
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods have achieved state-of-the-art results on a range of multi-agent tasks. Yet, MARL algorithms typically require significantly more environment interactions than their single-agent counterparts to converge, a problem exacerbated by the difficulty in exploring over a large joint action space and the high variance intrinsic to MARL environments. To tackle these issues, we propose a novel algorithm that combines a decomposed centralized critic with decentralized ensemble learning, incorporating several key contributions. The main component in our scheme is a selective exploration method that leverages ensemble kurtosis. We extend the global decomposed critic with a diversity-regularized ensemble of individual critics and utilize its excess kurtosis to guide exploration toward high-uncertainty states and actions. To improve sample efficiency, we train the centralized critic with a novel truncated variation of the TD($λ$) algorithm, enabling efficient off-policy learning with reduced variance. On the actor side, our suggested algorithm adapts the mixed samples approach to MARL, mixing on-policy and off-policy loss functions for training the actors. This approach balances between stability and efficiency and outperforms purely off-policy learning. The evaluation shows our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on standard MARL benchmarks, including a variety of SMAC II maps.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Evidence-Governed Deployment Readiness for Networked Agents on Industrial OT Infrastructure
Systems and Control (EESS).summary:
Deploying a workload on a cyber-secure industrial operational-technology (OT) network requires many cross-layer prerequisites to hold at once, including persistent addressing, name resolution, time synchronization, certificate trust, proxy traversal, and reachable industrial-protocol endpoints. These are owned by different teams, yet current tools treat pre-deployment checking, fault attribution, remediation, and ongoing compliance as separate problems, so evidence is rarely reused across stages. As edge platforms come to host self-adapting agents on shared infrastructure, this fragmentation becomes a governance problem. All four stages ask one question: do a workload's requirements hold on a given network?
  We present an evidence-governed framework that answers it through a single reference, a versioned network-intent artifact specifying a workload's cross-layer requirements for a specific release. A coverage-driven test loop attaches tested evidence to each requirement before deployment. At a site, readiness is reported as ready, not ready, or undecidable, separating untested requirements from genuine failures; a repair step proposes fixes that preserve co-located workloads; and a drift-watch component re-evaluates the site on change, extending assurance across the workload's lifetime. A multi-workload OPC UA commissioning case illustrates all four stages. By detecting runtime deviations and suspending an agent's guarantees until a refreshed artifact is registered, the framework grounds auditable governance for adapting agent collectives on shared industrial infrastructure.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Impact of Security Modeling Fidelity on Hyperscale Data Center Hosting Capacity Assessment
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper assesses hyperscale data center hosting capacity in transmission grids. Hosting capacity (HC) analysis quantifies the maximum additional load a bus can accommodate without violating operational constraints. This paper defines data center HC as the maximum time-invariant active power demand at a single target bus over a 24-hour peak-day horizon, and evaluates it under four models of increasing fidelity (i.e., the extent to which the model enforces real-world operational security requirements) on the modified IEEE 24-bus system: (i) DC optimal power flow (DC-OPF) without unit commitment (UC), (ii) basic SCUC (security-constrained unit commitment) without reliability constraints, (iii) SCUC with spinning reserve, and (iv) N-SCUC with both reserve and branch-contingency security. Comparing these models quantifies the impact of unit commitment, reserve requirements, and N-1 security on bus-level HC estimates. The N-SCUC yields an average HC of 444 MW; omitting N-1 security raises this to 532 MW, a 19.8% overestimation. The DC-OPF and basic SCUC models further overestimate HC, indicating a trade-off between model complexity and estimation accuracy.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Accepted to the 2027 IEEE PES Grid Edge Technologies Conference & Exposition

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Terrain-Aided Navigation Without Raycasting: A Sliding Grid Approach for Point Cloud Processing
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We investigate the use of a point cloud measurement in terrain-aided navigation. Our goal is to aid an inertial navigation system, by exploring ways to generate a useful measurement innovation error for effective nonlinear state estimation. We compare two such measurement models that involve the scanning of a digital terrain elevation model: a) one that is based on typical ray-casting from a given pose, that returns the predicted point cloud measurement from that pose, and b) another computationally less intensive one that does not require raycasting and we refer to herein as a sliding grid. Besides requiring a pose, it requires the pattern of the point cloud measurement itself and returns a predicted point cloud measurement. We show that the sliding grid achieves comparable accuracy to raycasting, especially at higher altitudes, while being orders of magnitude faster computationally. By eliminating the need for raycasting, the sliding grid removes the dependency on dedicated GPU hardware or high-performance CPUs, making it well-suited for real-time terrain-aided navigation on resource-constrained embedded platforms.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Impact of Data Center Load on Co-Optimized Generation and Transmission Expansion Planning with Embedded Unit Commitment
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: The rapid growth of hyperscale data centers challenges grid expansion planning, yet existing studies focus largely on operational flexibility rather than long-term investment decisions. This paper examines how large data center loads sited at multiple buses affect co-optimized Transmission Expansion Planning (TEP) and Generation Expansion Planning (GEP). The problem is formulated as a multi-year, Unit Commitment (UC)-embedded mixed-integer linear program on the modified IEEE 24-bus Reliability Test System (RTS-24) with Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT)-calibrated renewable energy profiles. A 500 MW data center load, about 17.5% of the base-year peak, is allocated across four buses by voltage level, generation headroom, renewable co-location, and network connectivity. Integrating this load raises the 15-year net present value of total system cost by 1,794 million USD (+61.6%) and the system-average locational marginal price (LMP) by 45.2%, with operating cost dominating capital investment (84.2% versus 15.8%). Renewable curtailment remains negligible: existing renewables are already near full utilization, so the added demand is served almost entirely by incremental thermal generation. Most notably, the load shifts the optimal plan from transmission-only to generation-only, replacing the base-case 230 kV reinforcement with a new 400 MW combined-cycle gas turbine and showing that strategically sited generation can substitute for network reinforcement.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Accepted to the 2027 IEEE Texas Power and Energy Conference (TPEC)

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Computation of Price Signals for Controlling Flexible Prosumers in Distribution Grids Incorporating Stochasticity and Fairness
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper proposes a method for distribution system operators (DSOs) to design spatially fair dynamic price signals for flexible prosumers, accounting for both distribution grid constraints and the stochastic behavior of prosumers. Since locational pricing can introduce price unfairness when grid constraints are active, the proposed approach includes mechanisms to enforce price fairness across the network. The method involves the DSO solving a scenario-based optimal power flow (OPF) problem to derive, similarly to locational marginal prices in transmission systems, the Lagrange multipliers associated with grid constraints and to compute individualized price signals for each prosumer under various PV generation and demand scenarios. Subsequently, two methods are introduced to aggregate these individualized prices into a single fair price across prosumers. Their performance is evaluated through simulations on a model distribution grid, comparing prosumer revenues, grid constraint violations, and analyzing the impact of fairness on reducing cost variance among prosumers.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Adaptive Handling of Deadline Misses via Stochastic MPC
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Real-time control systems may experience sporadic computational overloads that cause controller executions to overrun their expected deadlines, affecting the timely update of control inputs. Such overruns are classically handled with static decisions, e.g., by either stopping and discarding the late execution at the deadline instant, or continuing it while skipping the next activations. This paper first demonstrates that such static policies can lead to suboptimal performance when the controlled system undergoes varying operating conditions, and thus proposes a control-driven hybrid overrun strategy that optimally adapts the deadline miss handling at runtime. We model the closed loop as a Markov jump linear system, whose modes encode overrun histories, and we formulate a scenario-tree-based stochastic model predictive control problem that predicts and optimizes over possible sequences of deadline hits and misses. We evaluate our proposal on linear benchmarks including a double integrator and an aircraft pitch system.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Infrastructure-Aware Runtime Protection of Co-Deployed AI Services at the Industrial Edge
Systems and Control (EESS).summary:
In modern production lines, a single edge device simultaneously runs multiple AI services like a torque-control model, a vision inspector, a predictive maintenance routine. All these services run on the same CPU and same shared network segment. When the shared network segment saturates, the services do not crash. The services just produce outputs that are inaccurate or stale, and no longer reflect the plant's conditions. Our paper targets this class of silent, partial failure scenarios in Industrial Edge Systems.
  We treat each co-deployed service as an autonomous agent. We introduce the Runtime Criticality Score (RCS), which each service agent uses to express at any moment, its intrinsic utility and survival urgency under resource constraints. The score is computed from six normalized dimensions covering physical consequence, inference quality, input freshness, recent availability stress, actuator coupling, and available protective actions on the host. Its dimension weights are adjusted online through a lightweight Bayesian update driven by the type of disturbance currently observed, so the same service is ranked differently under a network delay than under thermal throttling. Agents publish their RCS to peers over an open, peer-to-peer discovery channel, and use it to negotiate three things without a central controller: (i) local threshold enforcement on their own host, (ii) migration to a willing peer when the current host can no longer protect them, (iii) reassignment of the coordination role when the incumbent coordinator is itself impaired. Beyond the immediate benefit of catching silent degradation, the framework contributes a concrete instance of decentralized, physically grounded agent coordination. Agents belonging to different owners can advertise capabilities, bid for protection, and reorganize across an open network.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Lyapunov characterization of boundedness of reachability sets for infinite-dimensional systems
Systems and Control (EESS).summary:
We prove a converse Lyapunov theorem for boundedness of reachability sets for a general class of control systems whose flow is Lipschitz continuous on compact intervals with respect to trajectory-dominated inputs. We show that this condition is satisfied by broad classes of semilinear evolution equations.
  For ordinary differential equations, as a consequence of our results, we obtain a converse Lyapunov theorem for forward completeness, without a priori restrictions on the magnitude of inputs. As an example, we rederive Wintner's classical result using our Lyapunov approach.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: BALLAST: Physics-Aware Moving Target Defense for Industrial Control Systems Using a Digital Twin Safety Oracle
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Industrial Control Systems run on static network configurations, which leaves an attacker unlimited time to map the plant. Moving Target Defense answers this by shuffling addresses, but almost every published scheme never checks whether the reconfiguration will itself disturb the physical process it protects, so the defense can destabilise a control loop or trip an actuator. We present BALLAST, which places a learned Digital Twin between the security policy and the plant as a safety oracle. A physics-informed LSTM surrogate forecasts the physical effect of a candidate network change, a reinforcement learning agent trades security entropy against process stability, and a connection-draining handover lets in-flight Modbus transactions complete before the old mapping is withdrawn. An explicit shield rejects any action whose predicted trajectory would leave the safe operating envelope. On the SWaT water treatment testbed, Ballast cut the success rate of an adversary's reconnaissance sweep by 85 percent and recorded no safety violation across 50 runs, a 95 percent upper bound of 5.8 percent on the violation rate, against five violations and a tracking error 19 times larger for RL-MTD, the closest published analogue to our design. Measured against the strongest baseline on the physical metrics, a threshold-triggered scheme that itself records one violation rather than RL-MTD's five, Ballast still improves the tracking error by a factor of 2.5 and removes that remaining violation. The gain costs a small and deliberate concession in raw deterrence. Twin inference meets the 50 ms budget on a workstation core and an embedded GPU, and is projected to meet it on both edge CPUs when the three envelope stages are evaluated in a single batched call; the complete decision-to-enforcement path was measured only on the workstation.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: On Over-Conservatism Under Low-Probability Extreme Events: A KL-Regularized Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Planning Method
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: The increasing penetration of renewable energy makes power systems more vulnerable to low-probability extreme events, elevating system planning to a critical role in ensuring reliability. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) based on the Wasserstein distance is widely used to address this challenge. However, we find that the conventional Wasserstein ambiguity set tends to excessively amplify the probabilities of low-probability extreme events, leading to over-conservative investment decisions. To mitigate this over-conservatism, this paper proposes a novel ambiguity set that modifies the Wasserstein distance with a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence regularization term. By leveraging the KL divergence's sensitivity to relative probability changes, the proposed set effectively curbs the unrealistic magnification of low-probability events. A two-stage distributionally robust planning model built upon this new ambiguity set is developed to optimize the installed capacity of photovoltaic, wind, and energy storage. The complex model is then reformulated as an equivalent exponential cone program with strict theoretical proofs, making it computationally tractable. Numerical results on the PJM 5-bus and IEEE 118-bus systems reveal the over-conservatism of standard Wasserstein DRO under low-probability extreme events and validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed planning model and solution algorithm.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Fast Analytical Method for Resource Adequacy Assessment in Renewable-Rich Power Systems
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper proposes a novel analytical method for resource adequacy assessment in renewable rich power systems. The approach begins by applying the stress strength method to estimate two key resource adequacy indices: loss of load expectation (LOLE) and expected energy not supplied (EENS). This method requires defining the probability distribution functions (PDFs) for both the generation side and the load side. The load is assumed to follow a normal probability distribution, while the generation side probability distribution is derived from the combined PDFs of conventional, wind, and solar power sources. The approach models the cumulative impact of uncertainties on resource adequacy using the central limit theorem (CLT), and improves accuracy with a cumulant based Gram Charlier expansion when the CLT alone is insufficient. The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated through Monte Carlo simulations conducted on the IEEE single area and multi-area RTS-96 test systems. The results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a substantial reduction in computational time, which is crucial in the context of operational planning, without sacrificing accuracy. Furthermore, its performance improves as renewable penetration increases, making it particularly suitable for future power systems operation and planning.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Data-Driven Surrogate-Model for Real-Time Loads Prediction in Floating Wind Farms
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This work presents a data-driven load-surrogate modelling framework for real-time control of floating offshore wind farms. The proposed methodology uses mid-fidelity simulations performed with OpenFAST and FAST.Farm together with MLife fatigue analysis to generate Damage Equivalent Load (DEL) datasets of floating wind turbines under wake steering conditions. A two-stage surrogate modelling approach is adopted: first, a Feed-Forward Neural Network (FFNN) is trained using data from simulations of a single floating wind turbine, while a second stage corrects the residual error between the FFNN predictions and FAST.Farm simulations using either Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) or an additional FFNN. The results show that the proposed framework can estimate DELs with errors generally below 15% for tower base bending moment, blade root bending moment, yaw bearing moment, and fairlead tension, while maintaining computational times compatible with real-time applications. The study also highlights the challenges related to generalization of the load-surrogate model under varying environmental and control conditions, especially for large floating wind farms. Overall, the proposed methodology demonstrates the potential of surrogate-based DEL estimation for load-aware floating wind farm control applications.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Generic Local Identifiability Does Not Imply Generic Global Identifiability in Linear Networks
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We give a counterexample to the implication from generic local to generic global identifiability for linear networks with a fixed topology, independently unknown edge coefficients, and selected excited and measured nodes. A six-node network with nine unknown coefficients has exactly two compatible parameter vectors generically. Adding six excited and measured nodes preserves this ambiguity while making the added coefficients directly recoverable. The resulting twelve-node structure has forty-two independent unknown coefficients and zero diagonal. For every positive bound on the largest eigenvalue magnitude, a nonempty open set of parameters has two distinct compatible networks satisfying that bound. This holds for both real and complex coefficients. Other open regions have exactly one admissible solution. The proof uses a rational transformation exchanging the two solutions and a common limiting matrix whose fourth power vanishes. Exact rational-number certificates verify an explicit pair. The construction also extends algebraically when the unknown coordinates are whole rational transfer functions. Genericity in prescribed numerator and denominator coefficient families, and the requirement that every transfer function vanish at infinite frequency, remain separate questions.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Estimating Closed-Loop Multiple-Input Single-Output Dynamic Systems using Gaussian Processes
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper extends complex Gaussian process regression-based transfer function (TF) estimation from the single-input single-output setting to closed-loop multiple-input single-output (MISO) systems. Accurate estimation of individual TFs in closed-loop MISO systems is challenging as feedback and correlation between measured signals can obscure the contributions of each input. We formulate a Gaussian process-based estimator for MISO systems, provide analytical conditions under which each system module can be separately identified, and show that the estimator converges to the true TFs in the zero noise limit. Moreover, we demonstrate how conventional closed-loop bias handling techniques relying on external excitation can be employed to construct appropriate regressors. Monte Carlo simulations support the analytical identifiability results and highlight the trade-off between closed-loop bias and error introduced by constructing exogenous regressors partly from endogenous signals. The presented work offers an expressive, nonparametric alternative to existing estimation approaches for MISO systems, while providing a probabilistic characterization of the estimation uncertainty.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Amplitude-Dependent Bode Diagrams via Scaled Relative Graphs
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Scaled Relative Graphs (SRGs) provide an intuitive graphical frequency-domain method for the analysis of Nonlinear (NL) systems, generalizing the Nyquist diagram. In this paper, we develop a method for computing $L_2$-gain bounds for Lur'e systems over bounded frequency and amplitude ranges. We do this by restricting the input space of the SRG both in frequency and energy content, and using methods from Sobolev theory. The resulting gain bounds over restricted sets of inputs are less conservative than bounds computed over the entire $L_2$, and yield three-dimensional NL generalization of the Bode diagram, plotting $L_2$-gain as function of both input frequency and energy content. In the zero-energy limit, the Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) Bode diagram is recovered, and at the infinite-energy zero-frequency limit, we recover the $L_2$-gain. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated on an example that resembles Phase-Locked Loop dynamics.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Control Systems Letters (L-CSS). This is the author's version, see the copyright notice in the PDF/source file

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Preliminary Exploration of Large Models Based on Self-Supervised Learning for Health Monitoring of Power Electronic Converters
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Current artificial intelligence (AI) methods for power electronics converters make limited use of the abundant unlabeled data generated during real-world operation. This underexplored resource holds significant potential for advancing model performance. To address this gap, this paper presents PE-TSFM, a time-series foundation model tailored for power module health monitoring. The model adopts the PatchTST architecture combined with self-supervised learning and is trained on more than 143 million timestamps, where over 98\% of this training data is unlabeled and collected directly from an operating traction converter. In degradation classification tasks, PE-TSFM achieves an accuracy of 87\%, considerably surpassing five conventional time-series AI models whose performance ranges from 27\% to 45\%. These results demonstrate the model's strong few-shot learning capability and generalization across different operating conditions. This work promotes a shift from narrowly focused models in power electronics toward unified, scalable foundation models that can unlock value from large-scale unlabeled operational data.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: Accepted by Proceedings of the 2nd Electrical Artificial Intelligence Conference, EAIC 2025

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Network Reconstruction in Consensus Algorithms with Hidden Agents
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Reconstructing the parameters that encode the influence between model variables based on time-series measurements represents an outstanding question in the theory of complex network-coupled systems. Here, we propose a solution to this problem for a class of noisy leader-follower consensus algorithms, where one has access to measurements only from the followers but not from the leaders. Leveraging the directed Laplacian coupling of such systems, we present an autoregressive expansion of the observed dynamics which can be truncated at different orders, depending on the memory of the leaders. When their memory is short, this allows one to correctly reconstruct the full dynamical matrix with hidden leader agents, provided some additional assumption on the system to lift the degeneracy in the reconstruction. We illustrate and check the theory using numerical simulations for the cases of both a single and multiple hidden leaders.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 4 figures in the main text, 3 figures in the supplemental material, 10 pages

Systems and Control (EESS).title: LiDAL-Assisted RLNC-NOMA in OWC Systems
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Optical wireless communication (OWC) is a key enabler for immersive indoor data transmission in future wireless networks. However, managing multi-user interference remains challenging in dense indoor OWC deployments with multiple optical access points (APs) serving multiple users. In this paper, we propose a dual-function OWC system for communication and localization. For data transmission, we design non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) combined with random linear network coding (RLNC): NOMA serves multiple users simultaneously via power-domain multiplexing, while RLNC improves decoding robustness under residual noise and processing impairments. The system is assisted by a light detection and localization (LiDAL) module that estimates users' spatio-temporal presence and location to enable dynamic user association. LiDAL also supports channel state information (CSI) estimation in realistic indoor scenarios where CSI may be noisy and/or highly correlated. We evaluate RLNC-NOMA by analyzing the probability of successful decoding and comparing it with conventional NOMA and orthogonal schemes. In addition, we derive the Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) to evaluate the localization accuracy. The results indicate that RLNC-NOMA increases the probability of successful decoding, and that the proposed unbiased location estimator achieves 44% better CSI accuracy than the baseline CSI estimation and improves the overall system performance.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: MagNav: A Dual-Core Magnetic Track Guidance Framework for Lighting-Invariant Navigation in Two-Wheeled Robots
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Two-Wheeled Inverted Pendulum (TWIP) robots are useful for studying how to control systems that are naturally unstable and have fewer actuators than degrees of freedom. Adding autonomous line-following to these robots is challenging because steering and balancing are closely linked. Most existing systems use infrared sensors, which can be affected by changes in lighting, such as sunlight or shadows, making them reliable only indoors. This paper presents a self-balancing robot that can follow a line using a magnetic track guidance system. By using a five-channel analog Hall-effect sensor array, the robot is not affected by optical interference. The control system uses a cascaded PID structure: the inner loop keeps the robot balanced using data from an inertial measurement unit with a complementary filter, while the outer loop adjusts steering based on the magnetic sensor readings. Stepper motors provide precise torque control without needing extra rotary encoders. For comparison, an optical sensor module was also included. Tests show that the magnetic guidance system keeps accurate tracking even in very bright lighting, over 10,000 Lux, while the optical system loses accuracy and sometimes fails. This design provides a reliable, lighting-independent solution for autonomous navigation in places like factories, warehouses, and outdoor paths.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 6 pages, 10 figures, 1 table. Accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Signal Processing and Effective Communication Technologies (INSPECT), organized by Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Patna

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Control Realization of Schrödinger Bridges over Discrete-Time Nonlinear Systems via Maximum-Entropy Distribution Steering
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper shows how a Schrodinger bridge (SB) structure emerges from maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) distribution steering of discrete-time nonlinear systems. We also establish that the resulting bridge can be realized by an optimal control policy. We consider general state and input costs, non-Gaussian endpoint distributions, and input constraints. Assuming the existence of a feasible policy with finite objective value, we show that the state-path measure under a MaxEnt optimal control policy is the unique SB. The reference measure of this SB is induced by an optimal policy of the corresponding terminal-unconstrained problem. Moreover, we give an equivalent characterization of the optimal state-path measure using a killed reference and its normalized Feynman--Kac measure, thereby interpreting the state cost as killing. We then characterize the finite-cost feasibility by the existence of an endpoint coupling having finite Kullback--Leibler divergence from the reference endpoint distribution. For compactly supported marginals with bounded target density, we derive reachability-based sufficient conditions guaranteeing this feasibility. We further provide specializations to fully actuated control-affine and reachable linear systems.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Enforcing a Strict Safety Margin in LLM Text Generation via Barrier Lyapunov Control
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed without formal guarantees against toxic text generation. Existing control barrier function (CBF) based safety filters can keep the generation trajectory within a toxicity-free region, but do not enforce a positive distance from its boundary, allowing formally safe trajectories to approach the toxicity threshold arbitrarily closely and leaving little buffer against modelling errors or disturbances. We address this limitation with a Barrier Lyapunov Function (BLF) safety filter that enforces a prescribed clearance margin throughout generation while retaining the continuous-time transformer dynamics, including feedforward layers. The resulting safe input set is a half-space defined by a constraint affine in the control input, and is non-empty under certified surjectivity and classifier-nondegeneracy conditions. For margin-compatible initial conditions we prove that the clearance margin is never violated and that the prescribed clearance is restored exponentially, yielding an explicit clearance floor, and show that, as the margin vanishes, the admissible trajectories satisfy the exponential second-order CBF condition. We further derive an explicitly computable sufficient disturbance budget under which the clearance guarantee degrades gracefully. Simulations on a small transformer illustrate the resulting improvement in safety clearance.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Safe Unicycle Navigation Among Multiple Obstacles Under Bounded Disturbances: A Learning-Augmented CLF-CBF Approach (Extended Version)
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper presents a robust control framework for safe navigation of a unicycle robot to a goal among multiple static obstacles under an unknown, time-varying disturbance. The controller solves a single real-time quadratic program (QP) that combines a goal-reaching term with one safety term per obstacle. The goal-reaching term is a cross-track control Lyapunov function built from body-frame tracking errors rather than a bearing angle, which keeps its Lie derivatives bounded everywhere, including the goal. Safety is encoded using robust control barrier functions, one per obstacle, each tightened by a closed-form, state-dependent disturbance bound. When stabilization and safety conflict, a slack variable relaxes only the convergence requirement, so that the safety constraints remain strictly enforced. Whenever the QP is feasible, the robust barrier constraints guarantee forward invariance of every obstacle's safe set under all admissible disturbances. Complementing this safety guarantee, a Lyapunov analysis yields an explicit ultimate bound on the distance to the goal. A learning-augmented variant replaces the fixed objective with a reinforcement-learning reference, which accelerates convergence when multiple constraints are simultaneously active. We further derive the obstacle separation below which the gap between two obstacles becomes too narrow to pass through under the robust constraints. For such gaps, a learned virtual goal for the Lyapunov function steers the robot around the obstacles without compromising safety. Simulations, a Monte Carlo study, and a comparison against a sampled-data robust baseline support the theoretical results.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Information-based Unified Design Framework for NMR Magnetic Tracking System
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) magnetic tracking offers a promising alternative to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based localization for medical robotic guidance. However, scalar field measurements and field-aligned marker moments constrain position and orientation tracking, requiring careful configuration design. We present a unified information-based framework that uses local covariance analysis to evaluate receiver geometry, marker separation, and external source configuration in on/off-board NMR tracking. Numerical evaluation shows that planar-array precision depends jointly on receiver count and geometry, with triangular lattice arrays achieving the lowest best-case position uncertainty among the evaluated layouts for 9--20 receivers. Two spatially separated, field-aligned markers enable device-axis tracking, with predicted angular uncertainty below $2^\circ$ at the evaluated workspace center for suitable marker separations. We further establish point-dipole source--receiver duality, unifying the analysis of on/off-board NMR tracking. These

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Transceiver-Integrated BD-RIS: Wave-Domain Signal Processing for Sustainable and Inclusive 6G
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: The shift toward sixth-generation (6G) wireless communications demands transceiver architectures that simultaneously support high-data-rate communications, pervasive sensing, and sub-meter-level localization. Beyond these performance targets, 6G systems are also expected to align with long-term societal goals, including sustainability and inclusiveness. Conventional radio designs, however, remain heavily reliant on digital baseband processing, whose cost, power consumption, and computational complexity scale unfavorably with increasing array size and carrier frequency, making them poorly aligned with these emerging requirements. Beyond-diagonal reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (BD-RISs) introduce a new paradigm by enabling direct manipulation of electromagnetic waves in the analog domain. This article presents BD-RIS as a wave-domain analog processing unit embedded within the transceiver aperture. By migrating linear signal processing functions from the digital baseband to the wave domain, BD-RISs significantly reduce computational load and energy consumption, enabling scalable and sustainable operation for extra-large antenna array systems. Owing to their ability to jointly provide high operational flexibility, modularity, and energy-efficient analog processing, transceiver-integrated BD-RISs offer a compelling architectural trade-off and emerge as a strong candidate for next-generation wireless transceivers.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Author-accepted manuscript. Accepted for publication in IEEE Wireless Communications, 2026

Systems and Control (EESS).title: A Programming, Robotics and Automatic Control Intervention for Secondary Education Students in Sweden and Italy
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This study evaluates the AutoSTEM workshop, an intervention for secondary education that combines a serious game with PID-controlled hardware. Seven workshops were conducted across Sweden and Italy. The six Swedish workshops adopted an explicitly SDT-informed facilitation framework, while the Italian workshop followed the existing educational robotics format without a formally defined SDT facilitation protocol. Self-reports, an objective knowledge quiz, and qualitative responses were analysed using multiple site-adjusted statistical approaches. Technical-specific self-efficacy increased substantially in both conditions, with large effect sizes, while objective knowledge showed only modest, non-significant gains. No significant site-adjusted differences were found between SDT and control conditions for the primary outcomes. Perceived engagement was higher in the control condition, although this finding should be interpreted cautiously. The objective knowledge composite remained positive but non-significant across sensitivity analyses. Female participants reported smaller PID self-efficacy gains than males. Qualitative findings supported evidence of PID learning while identifying technical and pacing barriers. Overall, the results suggest that the technology-rich intervention supports competence development, regardless of SDT-informed facilitation.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: This paper has 40 pages and 10 figures. Partial results have been presented at NPCW26 in Denmark and are available at https://npcw2026.compute.dtu.dk/Yamashita_npcw2026.pdf

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Service-Aware Hosting Capacity Assessment of Edge Data Centers with Workload Flexibility
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: The growing demand for edge computing, content delivery, and AI services is driving the interconnection of edge data centers (DCs) with distribution networks. Before interconnection, utilities evaluate how much DC capacity can be accommodated without violating feeder current and voltage limits. Fixed peak load representations can overlook service dependent demand patterns, cooling related facility demand, and delay tolerant computing tasks.
