Systems and Control (EESS).title: Autonomous fixed-wing interception using reinforcement learning
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Medium altitude, long endurance unmanned aerial systems such as Shahed-type strike drones are an unanswered threat in modern conflicts. Conventional air defense systems are too expensive to provide a feasible large-scale solution. Quadcopter interceptors are a cheap, battle-proven alternative, but their extremely limited flight time restricts them to low altitude targets at short range, whereas fixed-wing platforms have the endurance to reach higher altitude targets from longer distances. However, such interceptors are still operated manually. Recent developments in learning-based controllers show potential for automation. In this work, a fixed-wing interceptor is presented that is controlled by a neural network that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands. The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation. The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: MSc thesis, Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, Delft University of Technology, 2026. 24 pages, 29 figures, 4 tables

Systems and Control (EESS).title: FADE: A Flow-Based Approach for Multichannel Tail Estimation
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) is vulnerable to rare low-received-power events, and the spatial-diversity benefits of multiple receivers can be significantly reduced when they experience simultaneous deep fading. Multivariate Extreme Value Theory (MEVT) provides a principled framework for characterizing such joint tail behavior. However, conventional MEVT methods often rely on restrictive parametric assumptions or discrete representations of the dependence structure, which may not fully capture complex multivariate tail behavior. This paper proposes Flow-based Angular Density Estimation (FADE), a flow-based approach for characterizing the dependence between extreme events across receivers within the MEVT framework. FADE transforms multivariate extremes into a standard extreme-value representation and uses a flow-based density estimator to learn the dependence structure from the transformed data without imposing a predefined parametric form. The proposed framework is evaluated using experimentally collected data from a UAV communication system, in which the UAV serves as the transmitter and communicates with two ground receivers. FADE provides closer agreement with the empirical joint CDF, achieving reductions of up to 22.4% in MAE compared with the state-of-the-art Logistic and Maximum Empirical Likelihood (MEL) methods, while also improving distributional agreement and reducing absolute bias.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Distributed State Estimation over Wireless MIMO Fading Channels with Imperfect CSI
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We consider distributed state estimation of a linear plant under stabilizing feedback over wireless multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) fading channels, where channel-estimation noise corrupts the channel state information (CSI) used for information fusion. We propose a distributed estimator that combines local prediction, communication over wireless MIMO channels, and a posterior update based on local information and communicated data. Each sensor uses noisy pilots to estimate its aggregated wireless MIMO fading channel, and a pilot-noise bias correction recovers the required neighboring-data differences in conditional mean. We first analyze the mean estimation error and show that a Chebyshev design of the communication weights achieves a prescribed decay factor $d\in(0,1)$ satisfying the sensing conditions, with finitely many communication updates per plant sample at every finite signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) gain. We then characterize mean-square stability and the effects of SNR gain and receive-array size on the state estimation mean-square error (MSE), including its transient and steady-state value. In the ideal-communication limit, we show that the square root of the absolute MSE deviation from its steady-state value decays as $o(d^k)$. Numerical simulations verify the theoretical results and show substantial performance gain compared to various state-of-the-art baselines.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for Real-Time Electric Vehicle Charging Management in IoEV-Enabled Smart Cities
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: The rapid growth of electric vehicles (EVs) in urban environments demands intelligent, decentralised charging management strategies that operate under strict real-time constraints. This paper proposes an Edge-Intelligent architecture in which each EV selects a charging station (CS) by querying a shared, centrally trained Deep Q-Network (DQN) policy over a lightweight MQTT publish-subscribe backbone; independent per-EV edge inference is the deployment target, not the configuration evaluated here. The reported simulation evaluates that shared DQN policy applied sequentially to each vehicle's observations within a single SUMO run, using MQTT for KPI telemetry while observations are obtained through TraCI. The system is evaluated on two real-world road networks from OpenStreetMap (Rabat Agdal-Hay Riad and Tangier, Morocco); the primary network carries four geolocated public charging stations with heterogeneous power levels (50 kW and 150 kW). Three traffic demand profiles (morning, midday, evening peak) are simulated, and four decision policies are compared: an Adaptive Heuristic, a Tabular Q-Learning agent, the proposed DQN agent, and a Double DQN variant. A multi-seed statistical protocol (7 seeds, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Cohen's d) evaluates the results. The DQN agent achieves a 6.8% relative improvement in charge rate and a 5.4% increase in delivered energy over the Adaptive Heuristic under Evening Peak demand ($p = 0.016$, Cohen's $d = 0.99$ and $1.51$), while showing no advantage in waiting time; on the second network the heuristic leads on waiting time, so the ranking is not stable across geographies. A scalability analysis shows linear state-space growth with station count and sub-millisecond inference; all runs include intermittent station outages under a Markov failure process.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 17 pages, 4 figures. Authors' accepted manuscript (paper ID 733916, AI2SD 2026 cycle), to appear in an indexed Springer Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems volume. Earlier preprint version deposited on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22208979

Systems and Control (EESS).title: A sensor-driven physics-informed neural network for real-time occupant-centric space heating control
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Conventional space heating systems typically rely on single or sparse fixed-point temperature measurements, overlooking non-uniform indoor temperature distributions, transient thermal dynamics, and occupant-specific comfort requirements. This study explores an occupant-centric control strategy that aims to maintain the desired temperature around the occupant location. Spatially and temporally varying temperature fields, together with occupant mobility, make real-time local temperature estimation challenging. To address this challenge, we propose a control-oriented Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) model for indoor temperature-field prediction. Conventional PINNs rely on explicit time inputs and assume consistent temporal patterns across samples, which limits adaptability under variable initial conditions and heating sequences. The proposed model infers temporal dynamics implicitly from spatial coordinates and limited sensor measurements, improving robustness to changes in initial conditions and external disturbances. The method was validated across nine horizontal sensing planes in three controlled room-scale configurations. Against a validated COMSOL Multiphysics simulation, the PINN predicted the evaluated temperature fields with a maximum relative error below 1.85% across validation cases. These predictions supported an occupant-centric space heating control scheme. Compared with COMSOL-based offline control, the PINN-based system achieved an average prediction error of around 0.67%, and its rapid inference supports real-time occupant-centric control implementation. This work represents a move away from reliance on fixed-point temperature measurements in space heating control to an occupant-centric control strategy informed by real-time environmental feedback.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Direct Covariance-to-Beamformer Mapping for Low-Latency Hybrid ISAC Beamforming with Subsequent DoA Estimation
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems typically employ a two-stage beamforming pipeline, in which target directions are first estimated from the received covariance matrix and then used to compute the beamforming weights by solving non-convex optimization problems. Although effective, this approach introduces processing latency that can limit beam adaptation in dynamic environments. This letter proposes a beamforming deep neural network (BFDNN) for direct covariance-to-beamformer learning in ISAC systems. BFDNN is a compact regression network that maps covariance-matrix features directly to the hybrid beamforming weights produced by a hybrid ISAC beamformer, eliminating the direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimation stage during inference. Compared with MUSIC, classification-DNN, and regression-DNN based beamforming pipelines, BFDNN generates comparable beam patterns and higher effective spectral efficiencies while reducing the beamforming prediction latency by 25-30 times on the evaluated platform, demonstrating the potential of direct covariance-to-beamformer learning for low-latency ISAC beam updates. Moreover, the target directions can be inferred indirectly from the generated radiation pattern, yielding DoA accuracy competitive with that of dedicated learning-based methods in the evaluated scenario.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Constrained Sparsest Input Selection for Structural Controllability is NP-Hard
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We study the problem of selecting the fewest admissible input--state links that make a structured linear system structurally controllable. This objective counts nonzero entries from prescribed positions of the input matrix and is different from minimizing its number of nonzero columns. Prior work gives polynomial-time algorithms for several restricted cases, including single or dedicated inputs and prescribed input patterns satisfying additional graph-theoretic conditions. We give a polynomial-time reduction from perfect three-dimensional matching, establishing for the first time that the decision problem is NP-complete and the optimization problem is NP-hard. A refinement of the reduction yields an exact optimum relation and shows that the problem is APX-hard. An example also exhibits a strict integrality gap for the natural linear programming relaxation.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Multirate Data-Driven Predictive Control: Rank Obstructions, Identifiability, and Noise Conditioning
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We develop rank, identifiability, and noise-conditioning results for compact input--output predictors in multirate data-driven predictive control. The inverse of a square zero-input response matrix used in an existing compact-lifting construction is shown to be undefined under its observability and minimal-polynomial assumptions. We derive exact replacements using rank-complete data, characterize all predictor extensions, and establish the minimum-norm and minimax Euclidean noise properties of the canonical Moore--Penrose extension. A joint predictor is identified directly from mixed experiments with arbitrary initial states. Deterministic perturbation bounds quantify reconstruction errors through informative singular-value margins, while a positive-definite reduced weighting preserves the nominal quadratic cost. Sampling-rate observability and event-triggering analyses identify additional conditions needed for reconstruction and stability guarantees.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: QFabric: Guarded Cross-Domain Task Recovery and Its Limits on a Linux-RTOS Board
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Heterogeneous embedded boards pair a Linux application processor with a real-time microcontroller (MCU), which suggests moving a task between the two domains when its timing degrades. We present QFabric, a prototype that treats cross-domain placement as guarded recovery from a violated empirical soft real-time contract: a bounded task is compiled for both domains, monitored in windows with hysteresis, switched only after semantic and capacity admission at a quiescent epoch boundary, and committed or rolled back after probation. On an Arduino UNO Q (Cortex-A53 Linux and a Cortex-M33 running Zephyr), we characterize the stock Bridge RPC interconnect and measure five workloads in both domains under idle, CPU-load, and higher-priority SCHED_FIFO contention, with ordinary and real-time callers. Each MCU invocation costs about 19 ms of dispatch regardless of compute, the MCU runs the heaviest kernel 34x slower, and because every call traverses Linux userspace, Linux contention inflates the MCU path far more than the Linux path (p99 up to 400 ms versus 17.0 ms). Across 30 cells of a four-node chain, Linux meets every contract within 0.8% misses and QFabric correctly never migrates; a controller without hysteresis migrates in 7 cells, raising p95 by up to 177x, and probation rolls back 5 of those moves. On Linux-dispatched heterogeneous boards, migration therefore cannot isolate a task from Linux interference, and recovery guards matter chiefly by preventing harmful moves. This paper supersedes an earlier artifact release whose reported improvement arose from measurement defects that we identify. All source, raw traces, and generators are public.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23692354

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Feedforward Density-Driven Optimal Control (D2OC) for Tracking Time-Varying Distributions
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Tracking a time-varying spatial distribution poses a fundamental challenge for multi-agent systems, as agents often lag behind a moving target when reacting solely to the current target configuration. This paper develops a feedforward extension of Density-Driven Optimal Control (D$^2$OC) for dynamic distribution tracking with general discrete-time linear time-invariant agents. The proposed framework predicts reference sample trajectories along a known velocity field and incorporates these anticipated locations into the finite-horizon control problem. A scalar factor explicitly adjusts the feedforward action to account for predicted reference displacement. We establish an explicit receding-horizon control policy and provide a formal performance analysis that quantifies the tracking impact of prediction limitations. Furthermore, under a nominal stability condition, we derive explicit ultimate bounds on agent tracking errors and local Wasserstein distances in the presence of bounded reference drift, discretization errors, and transport perturbations. Monte Carlo simulations with linearized quadrotor dynamics demonstrate that incorporating feedforward compensation significantly mitigates tracking lag and enhances spatial distribution matching. These results offer formal analytical guarantees for predictive distribution tracking while preserving the computational efficiency and local optimization structure of D$^2$OC.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Dual Path Following for an Aerial Manipulator Under State and Input Constraints via Transverse Feedback Linearization
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper studies dual path following for a quadrotor carrying a three-degree-of-freedom arm. The center of mass of the combined system must follow a vehicle path and the end effector must follow a second path, while the arm respects its joint limits and avoids its singular postures. The vehicle and the arm are mechanically coupled, so one controller must handle both paths. With the center of mass and the end-effector path coordinates as outputs, and a dynamic extension of the thrust, the system admits a normal form without internal dynamics. We characterize the states where this normal form fails. We formulate the transverse feedback linearizing controller as a quadratic program that relaxes only the speed of the end effector along its path and imposes safety and actuator limits as inequality constraints. The program reduces to a scalar problem with a closed-form solution. If it remains strictly feasible for all time, the feedback is locally Lipschitz, both paths are invariant and attractive, and every constraint holds. In the physics engine Drake, the controller resolves a conflict between the two speed references by slowing the end effector while both paths remain invariant. By contrast, a cascade with a safety filter leaves both paths. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/am_dual_pf-/

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Uncertainty-Aware Joint Generative Modeling of Fault Event Sequences and Sensor Time Series in Solar PV Plants
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper presents a multimodal generative model designed to simulate a solar energy plant system for predictive maintenance and fault prediction. We propose a novel approach to enhance system generation through conditional generation by leveraging both event sequences and time-series data and improve next event prediction. The framework employs a Transformer Hawkes Process (THP) to encode event data and an iTransformer to encode time-series data, integrated via a co-attention mechanism that effectively captures cross-modal dependencies between discrete events and continuous signals. From these integrated representations, we employ two specialized decoders for simulation: a Conditional Latent Diffusion Model (CLDM) for modeling future sensor trajectories and the Score Matching-based UnceRtainty quantiFication for Transformer Hawkes Process (SMURF-THP) for high-fidelity event prediction. This dual-decoder strategy supports uncertainty-aware, history-conditioned simulation by rolling the model forward for a specified number of generation iterations, producing finite stochastic scenarios rather than deterministic extrapolations over the full observational record. Evaluated on a comprehensive dataset from the Red Rock Solar Site in Arizona, our approach improves aggregate event-prediction F1 relative to baselines and supports applications in predictive maintenance, fault detection, and energy optimization for solar power systems.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: Author preprint of a paper accepted to IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering; 18 pages including supplementary appendix

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Finite Global $H_{\infty}$ Optimization of the $Q$-Filter Time Constant for Nominal-Response Recovery in SISO Disturbance Observers under Parametric Plant Uncertainty
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper develops a finite real-algebraic procedure for global H-infinity optimization of the time constant of a fixed-shape Q-filter in a single-input/single-output (SISO) disturbance observer (DOB) under affine parametric plant uncertainty. Robust internal stability defines a possibly disconnected feasible domain, and the objective is the worst-case weighted mismatch between the uncertain DOB reference response and the nominal closed-loop response. A recovery-error factorization preserves affine dependence of the performance numerator and denominator on the same uncertainty vector. Phase lifting and a complex-polynomial Edge theorem reduce the uncertainty box to finitely many polynomial edges, while quadratic dependence of the squared frequency-domain inequality on the edge coordinate permits analytic elimination of that coordinate. The resulting semialgebraic formulation has only the squared frequency as a universally quantified variable. It determines the global infimum, decides whether it is attained, and constructs the complete optimizer set over the full robust-stability domain. A DOB case study with a plant family containing non-minimum-phase members yields a unique optimal time constant of approximately 0.0364075 and a worst-case norm of approximately 2.29975. The optimizer lies strictly inside the first robust-stability component, and every smaller feasible time constant in that component has a larger worst-case norm. Finite algebraic certificates establish robust stability, performance feasibility, and strict global optimality.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Differentially Private Distributed Optimization via the Intrinsic Randomness of Zeroth-Order Estimators: Sampling Geometry, Convergence, and Privacy Guarantees
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Distributed zeroth-order optimization has gained increasing attention in applications where exact gradients are computationally expensive or unavailable. However, the iterative exchange of local decision variables makes distributed networks vulnerable to inference attacks. While differential privacy provides a rigorous framework for privacy protection, conventional approaches generally require additional random noise, which inevitably affects optimization accuracy. In this paper, we investigate whether the randomness inherent in zeroth-order estimation can itself provide privacy protection. We develop a distributed zeroth-order gradient descent method that integrates consensus updates with a ball-uniform two-point gradient estimator. Our theoretical analysis shows that our algorithm attains standard convergence guarantees in both online and offline optimization settings. We then characterize the relevant probability distributions of the associated privacy mechanism, and establish differential privacy guarantees for both the online and offline optimization settings. These results reveal the potential of intrinsic zeroth-order randomness for privacy protection.

Robotics.title: Lifted Schrödinger Bridges for Gaussian Mixture Endpoints: Projection Gaps and Path-Space Obstructions
Robotics.summary: We study stochastic density control between Gaussian-mixture endpoint distributions under Brownian prior dynamics. Since the direct Schrödinger bridge between Gaussian mixtures is generally not available in closed form, we introduce a lifted path-space construction in which each trajectory is augmented with a source--target component label. Consequently, the problem decomposes into Gaussian component-to-component Schrödinger bridges with explicit marginal, drift, and cost formulas, while the mixture-level assignment reduces to a finite-dimensional entropic coupling problem with a Sinkhorn scaling form. We then analyze the projection obtained by discarding or forgetting the label. By construction, the projected law satisfies the original Gaussian-mixture endpoint constraints, but its relative entropy generally differs from the lifted relative entropy by a nonnegative conditional label-information gap. This gap reveals a path-space obstruction: the lifted optimizer cannot, in general, be identified with the direct unlabeled Schrödinger bridge after projection. We also derive the posterior-averaged Markov drift associated with the projected marginal flow, prove a kinetic-energy upper bound, and identify a common path-potential condition under which the projection gap vanishes. Several numerical illustrations showing density and shape control are recorded for a self-contained exposition.
Robotics.comment: 37 pages; revised version of a journal submission with a new section on duality certificates

Robotics.title: Tactus: Tactile & Pose Sensing Glove for Natural Dexterity Data Collection
Robotics.summary: Collecting naturalistic human manipulation demonstrations with accurate contact force and hand pose is essential for robot dexterous manipulation policy and foundational world model learning - yet no existing wearable platform provides both calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a form factor that preserves natural manipulation behavior. We present Tactus, a textile-integrated sensing glove that co-optimizes three design pillars: (1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5 mm fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation, (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies, and (3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable. Tactus includes a documented calibration pipeline for cross-glove consistency and per-session calibration for subject-dependent correction. To enable objective comparison, we introduce standardized benchmarking protocols for tactile force regression and hand pose estimation, and apply them to Tactus and two commercially available tactile gloves - to our knowledge the first quantitative cross-platform evaluation of this kind. Tactus resolves a minimum detectable force of 0.59 N at 95% confidence, 1.6 - 2.7x lower than the commercial baselines, and with 0.87 cross-participant consistency, while our pose tracking sustains 11.0 mm fingertip keypoint relative error during manipulation, when occlusion is heaviest. We show that these combined signals support object property estimation, slip detection, and representative recording of hand-object interaction - yielding demonstration data with the fidelity required for contact-aware manipulation policies and world models.

Robotics.title: Terrain-Adaptive Grouser Wheel for Optimal Planetary Exploration: Design and Experimental Investigation
Robotics.summary: Planetary rovers operating in extraterrestrial environments often encounter significant mobility challenges due to varying terrain features such as gradients and granularity. While recent works in multimodal wheel design have explored adjustments in stiffness, compliance, and diameter as a means to improve terrain adaptability, full wheel grouser-adjustable designs remain largely unexplored. Grousers are a compelling feature to actuate, as granular terrains tend to require increased grouser height for improved wheel performance. As a result, we introduce GROVER, a multimodal wheel capable of continuously adjusting its grouser height for terrain adaptation. Fixed-height performance was characterized on vinyl, coarse rock, pea gravel, and sand under two packing states. Across 950 trials, the best configuration varied with terrain, reducing slip by 34.6\%--58.0\% in granular terrains and improving travel time and energy consumption by up to 77.4\%. No single grouser height minimized slip across all terrains, motivating mid-traversal reconfiguration toward lower-slip operation. Two experiments demonstrated this. First, an instructed terrain transition changed grouser height toward a known low-slip configuration during motion, with slip decreasing by $44.0\pm4.7\%$ from the transient peak across 20 trials. Second, an online adaptation routine used closed-loop slip feedback alone to search the grouser-height range for a lower-slip configuration on four terrains with previously uncharacterized granularities: three field terrains and one laboratory regolith terrain. The controller selected different heights, with settled slip 25.4\%--37.2\% lower than the pre-settled mean. Together, these results demonstrate GROVER's ability to improve mobility by varying wheel morphology during traversal toward lower-slip operating states.

Multiagent Systems.title: MAPLE: A Multimodal Mobile Agent with Playbook-Learned Experience
Multiagent Systems.summary: Autonomous agents powered by vision-language models (VLMs) show great potential in navigating mobile graphical user interfaces (GUIs) to complete complex tasks. However, existing paradigms face fundamental scalability bottlenecks: fine-tuning requires massive high-fidelity datasets or prohibitive training time and compute, while gradient-free approaches rely on custom static heuristics or costly trial-and-error trajectory exploration where feedback is deferred until the end of execution. To address these limitations, we introduce MAPLE (Multimodal Agent with Playbook-Learned Experience), a novel gradient-free multi-agent framework that enables dynamic, step-wise experience sharing and execution-time prompt evolution. Unlike traditional action-reflection architectures that depend on costly, post-hoc self-reflection, MAPLE enables agents to cross-reference and distribute runtime insights in real time at each operational step. This dynamic exchange eliminates blind trial-and-error looping and steers agents along direct, grounded interaction paths. Extensive evaluations on the AndroidWorld and MobileWorld benchmarks demonstrate that MAPLE achieves state-of-the-art performance on complex, long-horizon mobile tasks, while proving scalable and adaptable across novel environments.

Multiagent Systems.title: On the Reliability Limits of LLM-Based Multi-Agent Planning
Multiagent Systems.summary: LLM-based multi-agent planning delegates operational decisions to specialists that communicate through finite reports. In this research, we study its reliability limits when a coordinator can revisit source records before completing a resource-constrained plan. A useful report can support an immediate decision or direct later reading, so its value depends on how these stages communicate. We derive exact communication and access tradeoffs and prove that two report forms suffice for a broad class of allocation requirements, one favoring immediate resource identification and the other distinguishing absence from unnamed availability. For shared capacity, this reduction permits joint optimization of reporting roles and adaptive reads for a fixed number of source types with unequal workloads and reading costs. Identical specialists can optimally report different facts, and maximizing immediate completion can impose an unbounded recovery cost penalty even with full-record access. We also conduct numerical experiments to quantify the benefits of the proposed joint optimization and show how source access improves language-agent decisions that already use their reports optimally. In particular, an exhaustive evaluation of 207,632 report designs on small allocation instances recovers the predicted joint optima. Our analysis suggests that reliable agent communication should be evaluated by the complete decisions it supports and the cost of finishing its unresolved cases, instead of solely by report length, local prediction accuracy, or immediate task completion, as is often the case in current practice.
Multiagent Systems.comment: 36 pages, including appendices; 2 figures. Substantially revised

Multiagent Systems.title: Speculative Ad-hoc Querying
Multiagent Systems.summary:
Large language models (LLMs) invite substantial effort and investment, yet agentic systems can spend much of their time waiting for tools. This paper explores how a small auxiliary LLM can reduce these waits by speculatively preparing a database while the primary LLM reasons.
  The challenge is that the auxiliary model must anticipate the primary model's actions before the primary model takes them. Our key insight is that database systems give the speculator a structural advantage: it need not predict the exact next query. Instead, it can prepare work shared by many plausible queries. Predicting query shapes enables advance compilation, predicting data access warms caches, and predicting broader data requirements enables precomputation of superset results that subsequent queries can refine.
  We present Wonder, a system that exploits this advantage for analytical SQL workloads. Wonder constructs reusable superset queries, materializes their components, and rewrites subsequent queries against the resulting temporary tables. Its scheduler prioritizes foreground queries while using reasoning intervals for speculative preparation. The same engine supports humans writing SQL, using incomplete queries to guide speculation and displaying intermediate results as they type.
  In a replay-based evaluation of agent workflows, Wonder reduces SQL execution time by up to 31.8% and combined primary-agent reasoning and active SQL time by up to 22.6%, with approximately 6% higher recorded main-agent and prediction API cost and 10% more read I/O on the full dataset. A separate 24-participant study finds significantly lower query latency on both analytical tasks and improved time-to-answer on one, with 87.5% of participants reporting increased productivity.

Multiagent Systems.title: What Does a Safety Label Measure? Auditing Situational-Safety Benchmarks for Multimodal LLMs
Multiagent Systems.summary: Situational-safety benchmarks label each scene SAFE or UNSAFE and score a multimodal large language model (MLLM) against that label, usually by judging its free-form answer, and these scores guide deployment. We ask what such a label measures. A label score can come from the scene, the request or the benchmark's own files. We propose the Benchmark Card, seven measured fields that tell them apart, and fill it for six benchmarks. Only MSSBench chat leaks the label through its image files: image size alone reaches 82.3% accuracy, matching or beating six of seven commercial models. Elsewhere the signal outside the scene comes from design. In MOSSBench the item partition fixes the label, and on HoliSafe the request alone ranks pairs about as well as the scene. On our corrected chat split, the size rule falls to chance. We then introduce the Spot-Stop decomposition, which compares ranking with labelling on pairs of a safe and an unsafe scene. It splits the gap above a label-swap null into three parts: a threshold part, overlap between safe and unsafe scores, and order that holds only within a pair. Most of fourteen open MLLMs rank better than they label, beyond what their AUROC predicts. On chat, one shared threshold repairs a third to a half of the excess, and label-free recentering recovers it on balanced batches. Recentering on unlabelled scenes of the same situation improves ranking on VSCBench for 13 of 14 models.

Multiagent Systems.title: Robust Safety Assurance for Robotic Swarms Using Decentralized Collision Verification
Multiagent Systems.summary: In this paper we present the methodologies, results, and analysis used to deploy a decentralized safety verification algorithm on a robotic swarm to prevent collisions at runtime in an outdoor environment. Typically, approaches toward verification of swarms of cyber-physical systems (CPS) are evaluated solely in numerical simulations or in highly controlled, noiseless indoor environments. Our efforts to implement collision avoidance on a real swarm system outdoors have revealed that the underlying algorithmic assumptions juxtaposed against the implementation details of the target system are critical factors in a method's efficacy in the real world. Here we modify, enhance, and analyze a decentralized reachability-based method for collision avoidance on a size, weight, and power-constrained uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) swarm with the objective of illustrating the challenges of real-world CPS deployments as well as provide guidance for researchers in this space. Verification performance, resource utilization, and timing data were gathered over the course of 140 total outdoor vehicle flights, including 6 swarm flights composed of 8 UAVs, and used to improve collision-avoidance performance as experimentation progressed. Our extensive experiments show that the proposed decentralized runtime verification approach can efficiently verify the safety of multiple UAVs in real-time and help all agents take safe actions to avoid collisions. On average, each agent, using our open-source safety_checker library, takes approximately 500-520 ms to verify its safety for the next 4 s into the future, in which the reachable set broadcast time dominates the total verification time (~300-500 ms).

Multiagent Systems.title: GURU: A Hierarchical Neuro-Symbolic Multi-Agent System for Verification-Aware Automation of Mission-Critical Digital Engineering and Operations
Multiagent Systems.summary: An AI can find a safe action faster than any human, but it must never decide what counts as safe. We present GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical digital engineering and operations, built on one partition of authority: learned models propose, rank, and accelerate; a symbolic rules engine checks every consequential action against hard limits before it executes; and validated physics confirms and decides. GURU runs a workflow as a closed control loop, with Navigation, Action, and Planning agents sharing one Common Internal Language and one training factory. Nuclear, aviation, and national-security guidance now requires this pattern; a harnessed language model keeps the model at the center, GURU puts a validated reference there. In computational fluid dynamics, the workflow raised the converged-simulation rate on unseen aircraft geometries from under 1 percent to 74 percent over 100 single-attempt cases, ran 54 live cases to Mach 6 on three facilities, and an ablation put the symbolic layer at 13 points of boundary-layer capture. Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters raised ParaView control success from 55 to 75 percent. In space domain awareness, where a language model cannot be trusted to decide, a frozen self-supervised world model under validated propagation scored highest of five methods at conjunction risk, including fully fine-tuned language models, with several-times-lower seed variance: the trustworthy design gives up nothing in accuracy, and the recipe transferred to reactor anomaly detection. A radar-to-avoidance debris pipeline was demonstrated in stages on a 2026 reentry; the hierarchy coordinates simulated teams of 200 aircraft. Training scaled near-linearly past 1,000 Aurora nodes and ran at 8,000. The approach extends to a control-grade microreactor digital twin with validated physics, not a learned model, as the safety basis.

Multiagent Systems.title: Surrogate Modeling and Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Complex Systems: A Workflow for Automated Simulation Exploration
Multiagent Systems.summary: Complex systems are increasingly explored through simulation-driven workflows that combine physics-based and empirical models with optimization and analytics. Despite their power, these workflows face two central obstacles: high computational cost from repeated expensive simulator runs, and limited transparency when decisions rely on opaque black-box models. We propose a workflow that addresses both challenges by training lightweight emulators on compact designs of experiments that (i) provide fast, low-latency approximations of expensive simulators, (ii) enable rigorous uncertainty quantification, and (iii) support global and local eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) analyses. This work formalizes a methodological bridge accommodating continuous, categorical, and integer variables across diverse domains, from engineering design to socio-environmental agent-based models. To validate surrogate explanations and examine how faithfully they reflect simulator behavior, we introduce a comparative methodology incorporating active validation filters, including explanation consistency and aleatoric uncertainty quantification. Furthermore, we provide practical guidelines for coupling experimental designs with emulator training to select architectures that balance computational efficiency with interpretability. We demonstrate the framework across two contrasting paradigms: a deterministic multidisciplinary design simulation of a hybrid-electric aircraft and a stochastic agent-based simulation of urban segregation. Results show that coupling surrogates with XAI enables large-scale exploration in seconds, reveals critical nonlinear interactions, and highlights potential design and policy levers while establishing consistent explanations across architectures.

Multiagent Systems.title: Personalized Rollout Allocation for Federated LQR Policy Optimization under Heterogeneous Process Noise
Multiagent Systems.summary: We study federated model-free learning of a common linear quadratic regulator (LQR) gain under a limited uplink communication budget, with clients that share dynamics and costs but experience different process-noise levels. Conventionally, clients transmit gradient matrices whose dimension equals the number of controller parameters. Exploiting the structure of two-point zeroth-order estimates, we consider an implementation in which clients transmit only one scalar cost-difference coefficient per rollout pair, while the server regenerates the associated perturbation directions from shared seeds. Communication thus scales with the number of rollout pairs rather than the controller dimension, turning the uplink budget into a rollout budget. Because noise heterogeneity produces gradient estimates of widely differing variance and every client carries equal weight in the fleet objective, uniform rollout allocation allows noisy clients to dominate the aggregated update and increases the probability of destabilizing updates. We propose a rollout-allocation scheme that assigns rollout pairs in proportion to the standard deviation of each client's estimates and show that it minimizes the variance of the aggregated update. The scheme is implemented exactly through a greedy integer allocation rule whose weights are estimated from the communicated scalars. We further prove that a single allocation factor quantifies its improvement over uniform allocation in a one-round instability bound, the certified step size, and the error floor of a joint stability and convergence guarantee. Simulations show that, under the same communication budget, personalized allocation reduces the one-step instability rate from $37\%$ to $0.3\%$.

Multiagent Systems.title: LLM-Augmented Agent-Based Simulation of Cyber Social Agents
Multiagent Systems.summary: Social media bots are often portrayed as malicious automations to be detected and removed, but automation on social media platforms encompasses a wide spectrum of roles, behaviors, and rhetorical strategies that can shape online discourse in both constructive and destructive ways. This work conceptualizes these automated actors as \textbf{Cyber Social Agents} through a taxonomy of archetypes characterized by their operational tactics and rhetorical style. We integrate this taxonomy into an LLM-driven social simulation, where agents communicate and coordinate in a network environment. Using empirically grounded CSA personas, we simulate heterogeneous online societies to study how agent diversity shapes information diffusion and social influence. Our approach bridges the gap between rule-based agent models and LLM-powered simulations with generated agents that are parameterized from empirical data.

Multiagent Systems.title: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads
Multiagent Systems.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate specialized agents to solve complex tasks, turning each user request into interdependent model and tool operations. Unlike independent requests, these operations become ready at different times and consume evolving context as agents coordinate and exchange results. This creates changing patterns of concurrency, computation, and memory demand that can expose different bottlenecks in LLM serving hardware. Yet benchmarking these effects requires capturing the collaboration rules that generate serving workloads, beyond the requests observed during execution. We present MAServeBench, a benchmark that treats multi-agent collaboration as a configurable dimension of serving workloads for LLM serving and hardware evaluation. Its composable stages capture how agents coordinate and exchange context in documented MAS workflows, enabling native executions to generate different workloads even when task inputs and tools remain unchanged. Hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve realized operations and dependencies for reproducible fixed-work replay and as inputs to architecture simulators. Task-linked measurements connect these workloads to serving execution and GPU/NPU hardware behavior, revealing why serving efficiency does not always translate into timely task completion. The benchmark code is available at https://github.com/ShengxuanQiu/MAServeBench.

Multiagent Systems.title: Autonomous Analysis of Thermoelectric Materials Big Data by Multi-Agentic AI and Construction of a Knowledge Base and Specialized AI
Multiagent Systems.summary: Extracting knowledge from large databases of experimental materials data requires repeated analyses and reusable records of their choices and results. We developed Multi-Agentic AI (MAA), a multi-agent system in which AI agents with distinct roles analyze experimental thermoelectric data under predefined instructions and quality checks, saving analysis records traceable to their sources. In four experiments varying theme and cycle counts, we measured what accumulated in these records. In the largest experiment (100 analyses across 10 themes and 10 cycles), concept co-occurrences were concentrated within themes, vocabulary was shared across themes and some relation descriptions were first detected in later cycles. A specialized AI that searches this experiment's knowledge bases and reads their analysis records answered materials questions with cited sources. Retrospective checks, including tracing an answer generated with a preliminary corpus back to the source data, exposed errors: traceability makes errors findable but not absent.

Multiagent Systems.title: Mixture-of-Models: Distributed Inference over Heterogeneous LLMs as Model-Level Mixture-of-Experts
Multiagent Systems.summary: Switch Transformers scale MoE model capacity by routing tokens in memory for one jointly trained model, requiring high-bandwidth interconnects, large memory, centralised ownership, and lack scalable composability. We propose Mixture-of-Models (MoM) architecture as Switch Transformer scaling to semantic level which composes inference across independently trained distributed LLMs, each run on its own GPU. The models reach joint consensus using N-Way Self-Evaluating Deliberation protocol: a combination of social-choice methods such as Delphi method and Quadratic Voting as well as Inference-Time scaling paradigm. We start with an empirical model that characterizes consensus as an inference-time trade-off between signal extraction and contextual noise accumulation, establishing a mathematical basis for convergence driven inference stopping strategies. We show experimental results where ensemble of smaller (<21B) models matches closely 120B MoE (GPT-OSS-120B) on AIME 2025 while larger ensemble of open-weight models reaches 90.0%, close to proprietary models at time of writing.

Multiagent Systems.title: Collective Reasoning, Single-Writer Execution: Fusion-MoA for Long-Horizon Agents
Multiagent Systems.summary: Mixture-of-Agents systems combine several language models into a stronger response, but tool-using agents act over long horizons in which every step changes external state and the history keeps growing. We present Fusion-MoA, a serving architecture that brings multi-model collaboration into this loop through executor-anchored consultation. One Executor model holds the full context and emits every text and tool call; when consultation is admitted, three specialist models review its proposed next action through a compact view under a shared 120-second deadline. The fleet sits behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so an unmodified agent client drives it as a single model. Fusion-MoA serves an in-car assistant and an in-car personal agent for intelligent cockpits and is deployed on MetaX C550 servers. Evaluated as four quantized open-weight models on five NVIDIA L40S GPUs and driven by Claude Code, it passes 78 of the 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, 16 more than its Executor alone and 29 more than a self-hosted quantized Kimi K3 on the same client. On the 63 tasks that both it and the API-served LongCat-2.5-Preview pass, it needs 14.5 minutes on average against 17.5. Specialist reviews use 0.4% of the Executor's tokens, and every tool call comes from the Executor.

Multiagent Systems.title: A Multi-Instance LLM Framework for Rating the Quality of Surgical Feedback
Multiagent Systems.summary: Verbal feedback delivered by attending surgeons in the operating room plays a critical formative role in resident trainee skill acquisition. Yet, assessing the quality of trainer feedback and its effectiveness in influencing trainee behavior during live surgery remains a challenge. Prior studies assessed feedback content relying on extensive manual annotation by expert human raters and focused on developing broad taxonomies that overlook the qualitative aspects of feedback delivery such as clarity or urgency. Limited existing automated methods, including keyword analysis and topic modeling, also fail to capture these nuanced aspects. We introduce a two-stage LLM-based framework that discovers interpretable feedback quality criteria grounded in the context of surgical training. Our method uses multi-instance prompting via repeated independent sampling of candidate criteria followed by consolidation, and surgical domain knowledge injection to discover a small set of human interpretable scoring criteria (e.g., Encouragement, Urgency, Clarity). These criteria are then used to automatically score live surgical feedback via an LLM-as-a-judge approach. Evaluation on 4.2k trainer feedback instances demonstrates that our AI-discovered criteria outperform prior content-based frameworks in predicting feedback effectiveness, including observed trainee behavioral adjustments and trainer approval. This work advances scalable, human-aligned assessment of communication quality in the operating room and provides a foundation for improving surgical teaching practices.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Lifted Schrödinger Bridges for Gaussian Mixture Endpoints: Projection Gaps and Path-Space Obstructions
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We study stochastic density control between Gaussian-mixture endpoint distributions under Brownian prior dynamics. Since the direct Schrödinger bridge between Gaussian mixtures is generally not available in closed form, we introduce a lifted path-space construction in which each trajectory is augmented with a source--target component label. Consequently, the problem decomposes into Gaussian component-to-component Schrödinger bridges with explicit marginal, drift, and cost formulas, while the mixture-level assignment reduces to a finite-dimensional entropic coupling problem with a Sinkhorn scaling form. We then analyze the projection obtained by discarding or forgetting the label. By construction, the projected law satisfies the original Gaussian-mixture endpoint constraints, but its relative entropy generally differs from the lifted relative entropy by a nonnegative conditional label-information gap. This gap reveals a path-space obstruction: the lifted optimizer cannot, in general, be identified with the direct unlabeled Schrödinger bridge after projection. We also derive the posterior-averaged Markov drift associated with the projected marginal flow, prove a kinetic-energy upper bound, and identify a common path-potential condition under which the projection gap vanishes. Several numerical illustrations showing density and shape control are recorded for a self-contained exposition.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Learning momenta for Hamiltonian-based models
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: There has been increasing interest in methodologies that incorporate physics priors into neural network architectures to enhance their modeling capabilities. Among these methodologies, Hamiltonian neural networks (HNNs) and their variants have gained considerable attention. These architectures explicitly encode Hamiltonian mechanics both in their structure and loss function, resulting in desirable properties and additional modeled information. A crucial limitation of HNNs is their reliance on data on the target system's generalized momenta. This severely hampers their applicability when the analytical form of the generalized momenta is unknown, which frequently is the case in real-world applications. The goal of the present work is to develop a general extension of Hamiltonian-based architectures that addresses this issue by simultaneously learning the system's generalized momenta, Hamiltonian structure, and dynamics from data. The proposed architecture learns the generalized momenta when their analytical form is unknown, and only (potentially non-sequential) data on the state and its derivatives is available. A dissipative mass-spring system, a double pendulum, and a rolling disk under nonholonomic constraints are considered as canonical examples to assess the performance of the proposed architecture.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Singular Perturbations for Control Systems Safety
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) offer a powerful theory for enforcing safety in dynamical systems. Yet, applying this framework to complex systems is challenging when subsystems are feedback-interconnected and operate at different timescales. Such structures arise naturally in multiphysics systems and in control architectures where physical plants interact with optimization, estimation, and control algorithms. In many of these settings, safety involves only part of the system, motivating the design of reduced-order certificates. Inspired by singular perturbation theory, we establish sufficient conditions, involving separation between slow and fast dynamics, under which a reduced-order safety certificate can be lifted to the full interconnected system. Specifically, we construct a composite CBF ensuring forward invariance of a lifted subset of the original safe set. We also show that the certified safe set expands monotonically as the tuning parameter accelerating the fast dynamics is reduced. Numerical results validate the approach on two robotic systems: a planar 2-DoF manipulator with motor dynamics and a 6-DoF UR10e manipulator controlled by a suboptimal optimization algorithm.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Sub Terahertz LEO Satellite Communication: Is Doppler Shift a Major Challenge?
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: In this work, we investigate the impact of Doppler frequency shift on sub-terahertz low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite communications using OFDM transmission. To comprehensively evaluate the severity of the Doppler shift impact on sub-terahertz satellite-to-ground links, we first put together an evaluation framework that jointly accounts for major Doppler-induced and non-Doppler-induced signal impairments in such systems. We then compare and contrast three possible engineering approaches to deal with Doppler shift in such a communication system. Our study concludes that (i)~while just ignoring the Doppler effect in such high-frequency and high-mobility systems substantially compromises the performance and reliability, (ii)~most of the negative effects can be eliminated by implementing only a small set of low-complexity measures. We particularly show that even a single Doppler shift estimation over a 5-min-long satellite pass over the ground user location may be sufficient to ensure high performance throughout the entire connectivity period. Hence, while Doppler shift is an important effect to account for in sub-terahertz LEO satellite communications, it should not constitute a critical design challenge for these emerging systems.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Differentiable Iterative Learning Control for Black-Box Position-Commanded Manipulators
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: High-accuracy repetitive tracking is challenging for position-commanded manipulators whose low-level controllers are inaccessible, while constrained model-based iterative learning control (ILC) can require substantial manual parameter tuning. We present Differentiable Iterative Learning Control (Diff-ILC), an online bilevel framework that adapts the parameters of a constrained ILC update between physical robot executions. A closed-loop differential model is identified once from paired smooth perturbations and subsequently kept fixed. At each trial, a constrained quadratic program computes a feasible command correction, while a real-anchored next-trial prediction defines a task-level objective. Hypergradients are obtained by implicitly differentiating the locally active KKT system, enabling multiple computational parameter updates without additional robot executions. Experiments on a 6-DoF DOBOT CR3 across unseen planar and three-dimensional trajectories show substantially faster physical-trial convergence than fixed-parameter model-based ILC. Across the four primary trajectories, after only two trial-to-trial updates, Diff-ILC achieves 78.8% and 76.4% lower mean joint-vector and Cartesian RMSE, respectively, than fixed-parameter model-based ILC.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Ranking the Parameters Shaping Grid Dynamics
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Generator and transmission line parameters do not shape the time-domain behavior of a power system equally; a parameter that dominates one dynamic property can be almost invisible to another. This paper studies how the physical parameters of a detailed and general nonlinear differential algebraic equation (DAE) grid model shape the properties that decide whether system states such as frequencies, voltages, and angles can be inferred, observed, controlled, and kept stable. The rankings are conditional as they depend on where grid sensors and actuators sit, on the operating region and the disturbance, on the network topology, and on other settings that the operator chooses. The framework combines DAE trajectory sensitivities, variational Gramians, and stability margin sensitivities to measure how much each parameter reshapes the network dynamics. On three benchmark systems, the rankings show where dynamic leverage concentrates and where the control-theoretic metrics disagree, and they point to how parameter studies can guide calibration, sensor and actuator placement, and security assessment. The proposed methods herein are also scalable and can be tested on grids with tens of thousands of buses.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Co-design of Output-Feedback Neural Network Control Barrier Functions and Observers for Stochastic Jump-Diffusion Systems
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: In this paper, we present a framework for designing controllers for partially observed continuous-time stochastic systems. We use the notion of control barrier functions (CBF) and provide an upper bound to the probability of state trajectories violating the system's safety when starting in an initial region. Our framework co-designs a neural network-based controller, an output-feedback observer, and a control barrier function for the given system. Although CBF requires full state information, we formulate CBF conditions over an augmented state space of actual and observer states. We train the neural networks simultaneously by defining appropriate loss functions, and finally demonstrate the effectiveness through two case studies: a linear DC motor and a nonlinear system.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Reduced Order Observers for Monocular Visual Inertial Odometry
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This work develops a reduced order observer framework of monocular visual-inertial odometry (VIO). The key idea consists in considering the gravity vector in the body-frame as an additional state and constructing an appropriate output that relates the monocular bearing measurements and their time derivatives to the body-frame velocity. This eliminates the need for the estimation of the landmark positions, leading to a six-dimensional linear time-varying (LTV) observer for the body-frame velocity and gravity, endowed with uniform global exponential stability guarantees. These estimates are subsequently used to recover the orientation almost globally, up to an unknown constant yaw offset, and the position up to an unknown constant translation. The mixed-bearing framework is further extended to account for the inertial measurement unit (IMU) biases, yielding a twelve-dimensional LTV observer endowed with local exponential stability guarantees. Numerical simulations are provided to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed observers.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Robust Safety Assurance for Robotic Swarms Using Decentralized Collision Verification

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Critical Inertia Estimation for the Three U.S. Interconnections
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: The rapid integration of inverter-based resources (IBRs) is reducing system inertia across U.S. power grids, raising concerns about frequency stability following large contingencies. This paper presents a simulation-based assessment of critical inertia--the minimum system inertia required to prevent first-stage under-frequency load shedding (UFLS) after the largest credible contingency--across the three major U.S. interconnections: Eastern Interconnection (EI), WECC, and ERCOT. Reduced-inertia scenarios are created by progressively replacing synchronous generators with IBRs, and dynamic simulations are performed using full-scale PSS(R)E and PowerWorld models. The results show that ERCOT reaches critical inertia at approximately 20% IBR penetration under the strict first-stage UFLS criterion--or approximately 58% if only the final UFLS stage must be avoided--compared with above 90% for EI and approximately 67%-68% for WECC. IBR shares in 2024 in the U.S. portions of EI, WECC, and ERCOT were 16%, 33%, and 44%, respectively, indicating varying proximity to critical inertia thresholds. These findings highlight the importance of full dynamic simulations to accurately estimate critical inertia and guide transmission planning under high renewable penetration scenarios.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: The Iberian Blackout: A Black Swan or a Gray Rhino? A Protection-Aware Dynamic Voltage Security Assessment
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: On 28 April 2025, the Iberian power system collapsed after a rapid voltage rise that led to widespread generation disconnections and loss of synchronism. The final report of the ENTSO-E Expert Panel attributes the blackout to several interacting factors including ineffective voltage control, fixed power factor operation, misaligned protection settings, manual shunt reactor switching, and limited observability. These factors raise a general question: given the current state, can the next trip, ramp, topology action, or shunt switching raise the voltages measured by overvoltage relays above their settings before voltage controls respond? We answer it with a protection-aware dynamic voltage security assessment. For each candidate event, the method computes the voltage at every overvoltage relay over the relay time window from a dynamic model of the network, its controls, and its relays. It predicts which relays trip after a first trip, identifies assets whose relay or measurement data are insufficient for a safety conclusion, and, when one exists, computes a minimum-cost fast reactive power action that keeps all relay voltages below their settings. Case studies on four benchmark systems and a 2000-bus system that reproduces the mechanism of the Iberian blackout show that the method flagged every event that caused a secondary trip within the relay window, never declared safe a plant that tripped within that window, and, on the benchmarks, found fast reactive power actions that prevented the trips within the relay window whenever it judged such actions feasible. These results were validated with nonlinear time-domain simulations. The code is publicly available.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Safe Unicycle Navigation Among Multiple Obstacles Under Bounded Disturbances: A Learning-Augmented CLF-CBF Approach (Extended Version)
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper presents a robust control framework for safe navigation of a unicycle robot to a goal among multiple static obstacles under an unknown, time-varying disturbance. The controller solves a single real-time quadratic program (QP) that combines a goal-reaching term with one safety term per obstacle. The goal-reaching term is a cross-track control Lyapunov function built from body-frame tracking errors rather than a bearing angle, which keeps its Lie derivatives bounded everywhere, including the goal. Safety is encoded using robust control barrier functions, one per obstacle, each tightened by a closed-form, state-dependent disturbance bound. When stabilization and safety conflict, a slack variable relaxes only the convergence requirement, so that the safety constraints remain strictly enforced. Whenever the QP is feasible, the robust barrier constraints guarantee forward invariance of every obstacle's safe set under all admissible disturbances. Complementing this safety guarantee, a Lyapunov analysis yields an explicit ultimate bound on the distance to the goal. A learning-augmented variant replaces the fixed objective with a reinforcement-learning reference, which accelerates convergence when multiple constraints are simultaneously active. We further derive the obstacle separation below which the gap between two obstacles becomes too narrow to pass through under the robust constraints. For such gaps, a learned virtual goal for the Lyapunov function steers the robot around the obstacles without compromising safety. Simulations, a Monte Carlo study, and a comparison against a sampled-data robust baseline support the theoretical results.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Benchmarking Classical Machine Learning Models for Shading-Fault Detection in Rooftop Photovoltaic Systems Using Real Sensor Data
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Most published comparisons of machine-learning classifiers for photovoltaic (PV) fault detection are validated on simulated faults. We compare seven classical and ensemble-tree classifiers on the Réunion dataset, a 4 kW domestic rooftop plant on which shading faults were physically staged and logged. Readings within a staged episode are near-duplicates, so every train/test split is grouped by episode. A 20,800-row subsample that retains all 17 fault episodes was evaluated with three repeats of five-fold group-aware nested cross-validation, with synthetic minority oversampling (SMOTE) applied inside the training folds. Random Forest and XGBoost gave the highest mean accuracy (0.838 and 0.831) and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC; 0.526 and 0.522). After Holm correction across the 21 pairwise Wilcoxon tests, only Random Forest's accuracy advantage over k-nearest neighbours and the multi-layer perceptron remained significant. Logistic Regression and the Decision Tree (accuracy 0.820) could be separated neither from the ensembles nor from the weakest models. SMOTE lowered binary MCC for six of the seven classifiers. Errors were concentrated in whole episodes: the Random Forest almost entirely missed four of the 17 fault episodes, including one of two uniform-shading and two of five intermittent-shading episodes. A post-hoc diagnostic shows that the no-fault rows were sampled over a wider range of times of day and output levels than the fault rows. Clock time alone reaches an MCC of 0.44, and PV-side voltage alone 0.72. The reported scores therefore reflect operating-condition differences as well as shading signatures. We release the pipeline and the diagnostics, and identify matched no-fault sampling as the step needed before the classifier ranking can be generalised.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Robust Data-Driven Output Feedback for Systems With Unknown Input Delays
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: In a history-feedback realization, an input delay increases memory without increasing the number of unknown physical coefficients. We use this structure to design output-feedback controllers for discrete-time systems with one input, one output, and known undelayed order, using noisy input-output data. For a known delay, we derive a necessary and sufficient linear matrix inequality for common-quadratic stabilization of all models consistent with the data. Optimizing its equation-error bound gives a robustness margin for the measured record. For an unknown constant delay in a known interval, we characterize noiseless delay ambiguity and give a sufficient condition for one controller to stabilize all models for every delay consistent with the error bound. Under stated excitation and nondegeneracy assumptions, this procedure is feasible for all sufficiently small equation errors. Numerical examples compare robustness at equal controller memory and show that certified stabilization can succeed while distinct delay models remain compatible with the same data.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Submitted jointly to IEEE Control Systems Letters (L-CSS)

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Learning hidden-state dynamics from unpaired snapshots with lift-project SDEs
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Many systems are observed only through unpaired snapshots, with population samples available at each time point but no correspondence between samples at different times. These snapshots determine the one-time distributions but leave the temporal coupling unspecified, requiring a modeling prior to connect successive times. We propose the lift-project stochastic differential equation (SDE), an autonomous SDE on the observed coordinate and a few hidden coordinates, trained only to match the snapshots. Most existing methods, including time-dependent SDEs, Schrödinger bridges and optimal transport, evolve the observed coordinate alone. For a scalar observation, the classical comparison theorem implies that all such models have non-negative lagged covariance, so on data whose lagged covariance turns negative, their error has a computable floor. The lift-project SDE is not bound by this floor. On two representative partially observed systems, the Duffing and pendulum oscillators, at comparable fit to the snapshots, the proposed method reduces the lagged-covariance error by factors of 2.4 and 6.6 relative to the strongest baseline and is the only model below the error floor; one hidden coordinate is already enough for such improvement. Furthermore, if a second experiment changes only the initial state of the hidden coordinate, no single model that evolves the observed coordinate alone can fit both experiments, whereas a single lift-project SDE can.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Vision-based Sensing of Urban Environment using Hardware-Software co-design at Scale
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Urban environmental monitoring is crucial for climate-adaptive cities, yet current approaches rely heavily on human inspection, overhead remote sensing, or limited terrestrial RGB imagery, thereby lacking comprehensive multispectral perspectives at street level. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces UrbanScapes, an adaptable and flexible hardware-software co-design platform for large-scale, vision-based sensing of urban environments. Built on a modular architecture, UrbanScapes seamlessly integrates multispectral imaging channels, including Red, Green, Blue (RGB), Near-Infrared, and Thermal, to capture multispectral street-level imagery. The system is designed for both opportunistic deployment on bicycles, vehicles, or pedestrians and targeted deployments on municipal fleets, ensuring high spatio-temporal scalability without requiring hardware redesigns. Crucially, the platform utilizes on-device deep learning models to automatically remove personally identifiable information (PII) at the edge, addressing privacy concerns inherent in street-level data collection. By combining this multispectral street-level imagery with overhead multispectral remote sensing imagery, UrbanScapes enables scalable calculation of physics-based environmental indices, providing a foundational tool for advanced citywide analysis.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: IEEE World Forum for Internet of Things 2026

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Deep Reinforcement Learning with Smith-Predictor Delay Compensation
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Time delays can degrade feedback performance and destabilize a closed loop that is stable without delay. This paper studies Smith-predictor-assisted reinforcement learning for systems with constant input delays. A deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) actor is trained on a nominal delay-free environment and deployed with a Smith predictor using a fixed nominal delay. For linear controllers, we derive exact closed-loop maps under plant and delay mismatch and provide small-gain and $ν$-gap robustness conditions. A separate delay-independent Razumikhin condition gives a sufficient stability test for a fixed Lipschitz state-feedback policy. We also study output-error delay identification from a fixed input--output record, deriving the loss gradient and establishing projected-flow descent and local exponential convergence under exact model matching and an excitation condition. These identification results do not imply stability of an online adaptive predictor. Numerical experiments retained from the conference study compare PID, LQR, and DDPG controllers on stable and open-loop unstable first-order plants with valve stiction. The results illustrate the benefit of predictor compensation in the tested configurations and the sensitivity of standalone DDPG to delay and plant changes.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: This is an extended version of the paper published in the proceedings of IEEE American Control Conference (ACC)

Systems and Control (EESS).title: DiffGIPC: Differentiable Mixed-Coordinate Contact Mechanics on GPU
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Contact-rich inverse problems require efficient gradients and reliable enforcement of non-penetration. Existing differentiable methods provide fast simulation and rigid-deformable coupling, but contact treatments based on penalties or velocity-level constraints can permit penetration or positional drift. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) maintains non-penetration through geometric barriers and {continuous collision detection (CCD)}. However, repeated forward and backward evaluations remain costly in full-space finite-element (FEM) implementations, particularly when nearly rigid components retain many vertex {degrees of freedom (DoFs)}. We present DiffGIPC, a GPU-accelerated differentiable IPC framework for optimizing interacting deformable and nearly rigid bodies. Our affine-body derivatives enable {rest-shape} design, initial-state optimization, and articulated control while retaining only twelve motion DoFs per affine body. These gradients account for how changes in geometry, placement, and actuation affect other objects through collision and friction. We preserve these interactions in one coupled FEM-affine adjoint system per frame, reducing the backward-system size without discarding the dependencies that drive the inverse problem. GPU-optimized backward computation further reduces the cost of repeated gradient evaluations. A reusable PyTorch interface connects supported physical parameters to user-defined parameter maps and losses across design, identification, motion, placement, and articulated control. Experiments demonstrate peak speedups over DiffIPC of approximately 150.0x with full-space FEM and 4133.3x with affine bodies for combined forward simulation and backward differentiation.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Mixture-of-Models: Distributed Inference over Heterogeneous LLMs as Model-Level Mixture-of-Experts
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Switch Transformers scale MoE model capacity by routing tokens in memory for one jointly trained model, requiring high-bandwidth interconnects, large memory, centralised ownership, and lack scalable composability. We propose Mixture-of-Models (MoM) architecture as Switch Transformer scaling to semantic level which composes inference across independently trained distributed LLMs, each run on its own GPU. The models reach joint consensus using N-Way Self-Evaluating Deliberation protocol: a combination of social-choice methods such as Delphi method and Quadratic Voting as well as Inference-Time scaling paradigm. We start with an empirical model that characterizes consensus as an inference-time trade-off between signal extraction and contextual noise accumulation, establishing a mathematical basis for convergence driven inference stopping strategies. We show experimental results where ensemble of smaller (<21B) models matches closely 120B MoE (GPT-OSS-120B) on AIME 2025 while larger ensemble of open-weight models reaches 90.0%, close to proprietary models at time of writing.

Robotics.title: DreamX: Video Diffusion Model is a Universal Latent Action Learner
Robotics.summary: Learning a universal action representation from video requires modeling dynamics that are consistent across different executions of the same action yet invariant to changes in embodiment and appearance. Existing latent action models infer actions from visual transitions, but their representations often entangle the underlying action with irrelevant visual variations, limiting transfer across embodiments. We introduce DreamX, which repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a universal latent action learner. Our approach extracts compact latent actions from the video model's rich spatiotemporal features, compressing each latent video frame by $\boldsymbol{300\times}$ ($\boldsymbol{1{,}200 \rightarrow 4}$ tokens). In addition, by leveraging the video model's generative prior, these latent actions capture action-relevant dynamics disentangled from visual appearance. The resulting latent space serves as a shared action interface across embodiments (human and robot), environments, and action parameterizations. On LARY-Bench, DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models. Moreover, actions encoded in one setting remain effective in another: the latent space supports any-to-any video transfer and zero-shot action transfer across diverse embodiments and environments. Furthermore, this shared interface also enables policy learning in a compact latent action space, reducing the computational cost of video-diffusion-based policies.
